title: Turn on hart1's branch predictor, BTB and return-address stack (MHCR 0x7c1) — Linux's CPU0 currently runs with all three off
layer: hart0 loader (bootloader/main/core1_trampoline.S) or OpenSBI hart init (platform/generic/espressif/esp32s31.c)
mechanism: The S31 core has a branch-target buffer, a predictive-jump unit and an address return stack, all gated by three bits in the M-mode CSR MHCR (0x7c1): MHCR_RS (1<<4), MHCR_BFE (1<<5), MHCR_BTB (1<<12). ESP-IDF turns them on unconditionally on every core it brings up, in call_start_cpu1() for the secondary core and in init_cpu() for the primary. Our loader does NOT use IDF's secondary-core path: core1_trampoline.S is entered directly from the core1 boot-address register and replaces call_start_cpu1() wholesale. It programs mie, mtvec, mtvt, mstatus.MPRV, the 128 CLIC slots, pmacfg7/pmaaddr7 and pmpcfg0/pmpaddr0, then jumps to 0x40380000 — and never writes 0x7c1. OpenSBI's S31 platform does not write it either. So hart0 (lent to Linux as CPU1) runs with prediction enabled, and hart1 (Linux CPU0 — 86% of Quake's main thread, every device IRQ, all of the kernel entry path) runs with the front end unpredicted. Fix: three CSR bits set once in the trampoline before the jump to OpenSBI, or in OpenSBI's per-hart early init. Verify first by reading 0x7c1 in M-mode on both harts — the project already does exactly this kind of M-mode CSR probe (it established that 0x7F2/PIE reads back 0 on hart0).
evidence: /opt/esp-idf/components/riscv/include/riscv/rv_utils.h: `#define MHCR 0x7c1`, `MHCR_RS (1<<4) /* address return stack */`, `MHCR_BFE (1<<5) /* allow predictive jump */`, `MHCR_BTB (1<<12) /* branch target prediction enable */`; rv_utils_en_branch_predictor() at line 555 does `RV_SET_CSR(MHCR, MHCR_RS|MHCR_BFE|MHCR_BTB)`.

/opt/esp-idf/components/esp_system/port/cpu_start.c:244 — esp_cpu_branch_prediction_enable() inside call_start_cpu1() (the secondary-core entry), and :437 inside init_cpu() for the primary. Both are `#if SOC_BRANCH_PREDICTOR_SUPPORTED`, and /Users/gadyke/esp32-s31-linux/bootloader/sdkconfig has CONFIG_SOC_BRANCH_PREDICTOR_SUPPORTED=y.
/Users/gadyke/esp32-s31-linux/bootloader/main/core1_trampoline.S: the full hart1 entry sequence, with no write to 0x7c1 anywhere.

grep -rniE 'mhcr|0x7c1|branch_pred' over the repo returns only unrelated vendor OpenSBI platforms (thead/c9xx_encoding.h, spacemit/k1.h, allwinner/sun20i-d1.c) and two false positives in prboom's r_filter.h. opensbi-esp32-s31/platform/generic/espressif/esp32s31.c does write 0x7f1/0x7f2 and read 0x7c6-0x7cb, so M-mode CSR pokes on hart1 are already routine there.

That IDF calls the enable on every core start is itself evidence the reset default is not fully on; mspi_timing_tuning.c and panic_handler.c bracket cache-disabled windows with disable/enable pairs, i.e. it is on during normal IDF operation.
magnitude_estimate: Unknown until 0x7c1 is read back, but this is a whole-core front-end feature, not a path-local one. On a 320 MHz in-order RISC-V, restoring a BTB + return stack is typically 5-15% on branchy integer code. Quake's CPU0 samples are 59% user + 32% kernel, so a 10% execution-rate gain is roughly +6-9% end to end — the same order as the .text..fast win, for three CSR bits and zero RAM. Against the ±10% per-boot lottery this needs 3-4 fresh boots per arm.
rule_check: No application binary touched (a CSR bit affects whatever runs on the hart). Apps stay on SD. Nothing disabled. No upstream code patched — the change is in our own trampoline/OpenSBI. Zero RAM cost, so the 15.4 MB constraint is untouched. Reversible by clearing the same bits.
prior_attempts: Not in the dead-end register. The nearest entries are #17 (I-cache autoload via devmem/loader) and #62 (the PIE/HWLoop coprocessor hook) — both different registers with different failure modes. Nothing in docs/ or the memory index mentions MHCR or branch prediction.

title: Enable the I-cache hardware prefetcher (autoload) for hart1 over the kernel's flash text window — dead end #17 was closed on a misread register
layer: hart0 loader (bootloader/main/main.c, at the existing prepare_core1_cached_psram() cache-register block, before hart1 is released)
mechanism: The S31 cache controller has a hardware autoload (prefetch) engine per cache: two address sections for each I-cache, four for the D-cache, with a trigger mode of miss / hit / both and an ascending or descending walk. For hart1 the registers are CACHE_L1_ICACHE1_AUTOLOAD_CTRL (0x2C0000FC), SCT0_ADDR (0x100), SCT0_SIZE (0x104, 28-bit), SCT1 at 0x108/0x10c. Point section 0 at the kernel's flash XIP text window and enable ENA|SCT0_ENA with TRIGGER_MODE=miss, so the engine runs ahead of the fetch unit on the flash bus. This attacks exactly the cost that .text..fast attacks (a 64 B line fill from 80 MHz QIO flash is ~2 us against a 320 MHz core) but costs zero PSRAM and does not compete for the shared D-cache. The register write must happen from hart0 in the loader, at the point where main.c already clears CACHE_L1_ICACHE_SHUT_IBUS1 and CACHE_L1_DCACHE_SHUT_DBUS0 for hart1 — hart1 is not running yet, so there is no self-reconfiguration hazard. The ROM also exposes Cache_Config_L1_CORE1_ICache_Autoload() / Cache_Enable_L1_CORE1_ICache_Autoload() for this, which is the API the earlier attempt should have used.
evidence: /opt/esp-idf/components/soc/esp32s31/register/soc/cache_reg.h:2165 — CACHE_L1_ICACHE1_AUTOLOAD_CTRL_REG; `AUTOLOAD_ENA : R/W; bitpos: [0]; default: 0` and `AUTOLOAD_DONE : RO; bitpos: [1]; default: 1`. Dead end #17 recorded 'the register still reads 0x2' and concluded the feature was already on — 0x2 is DONE=1 with ENA=0, i.e. the prefetcher has never been enabled. The memory note s31-icache-autoload-wedges agrees with the register: 'the S31 prefetcher is off on both harts'.

/opt/esp-idf/components/hal/esp32s31/include/hal/cache_ll.h:211 — cache_ll_l1_enable_icache() passes the autoload flag to ROM Cache_Enable_L1_CORE1_ICache(), which only applies it on a disabled→enabled transition. That is why the loader-side attempt was a no-op: the cache was already enabled. cache_hal.c:48-51 merely *reads back* whatever autoload state it finds and never turns it on.

/Users/gadyke/esp32-s31-linux/bootloader/main/main.c:282-284 already does raw REG_CLR_BIT on CACHE_L1_ICACHE_CTRL_REG / CACHE_L1_DCACHE_CTRL_REG for hart1 at this exact point, so the access path and timing are proven.
Same file, cache_ll_l1_invalidate_icache_addr(1, ...) — cache_id 1 is hart1, confirming which of ICACHE0/ICACHE1 to program.

DR_REG_CACHE_BASE = 0x2C000000 (reg_base.h:114), inside the CPU-peripheral aperture 0x2C000000-0x2C020000 — not the 0x20100000+ peripheral window Linux maps, which is a plausible reason the S-mode attempt in #17 'killed the hart instantly, twice'.

The four-section D-cache autoload (CACHE_L1_DCACHE_AUTOLOAD_CTRL, 0x2C000138, ENA default 0) is the same knob for PSRAM data, and is the obvious second arm given CPU PSRAM copy measures 102 MB/s against GDMA's 210.
magnitude_estimate: Targets the biggest lever the project has found (kernel XIP text is 5.98x slower from flash than RAM; 113 KB moved to .text..fast took the timer IRQ 0.864→0.465 ms and SD 12.07→8.05 ms). A prefetcher cannot beat resident RAM text, but it applies to all 4.38 MB of flash text rather than a hand-picked 40-110 KB, and costs no RAM. Expect a few percent on kernel-heavy paths if it works at all; the honest answer is that the knob has never actually been turned on, so the value is unmeasured rather than small. Risk of a loss: a prefetcher on a shared flash bus can add bus contention against the SD/scanout DMA, so measure SD p50 as well as fps.
rule_check: No app rebuilt or steered. Apps stay on SD and their paging is untouched (they page into PSRAM, not flash). Nothing disabled. No upstream kernel/Xorg/mesa code patched — the write is in our loader. Zero RAM cost.
prior_attempts: Dead end #17: 'I-cache autoload via devmem from Linux, or via cache_ll_l1_enable_icache in the loader — From Linux: the hart died instantly, twice. From the loader: a no-op, the register still reads 0x2, because the flag only applies when the cache is enabled and it is already on.' Reopened because the stated cause is wrong in two ways: 0x2 is DONE (default 1), not ENA (default 0), so the register was reporting 'off, idle'; and the loader route used the enable-cache wrapper instead of the autoload config/enable pair. Rollback image hello_world.PRE-AUTOLOAD.bin still exists.

title: Run the flash at 120 MHz instead of 80 — the esp32s31 MSPI timing-tuning port exists in this IDF, which is the fact dead end #26 was closed on
layer: ESP-IDF build of the hart0 loader (spi_flash/esp32s31/Kconfig.flash_freq + mspi_timing_tuning/port/esp32s31)
mechanism: Every kernel I-cache miss and every cold userspace XIP page is a 64 B line fill over the flash bus; at 80 MHz QIO that is ~2 us, ~640 CPU cycles at 320 MHz, and it is the documented root of the 6x penalty. The S31 silicon supports MSPI timing tuning by DQS and IDF v6.1-dev ships an esp32s31 port whose mspi_timing_config_set_flash_clock() already implements the 120 MHz path — it selects SPLL/4, asserts core_clock_mhz == 120, sets the flash bus divider and masks invalid DQS. Two things are missing: the 120M entry in the S31 flash-frequency Kconfig choice (it offers only 20/40/80), and the CORE_CLK_120M_MODULE_CLK_120M_STR_MODE tuning table, which is byte-identical across the P4, C5 and C61 ports. The tuning routine is self-validating: it writes/reads MSPI_TIMING_TEST_DATA_LEN words at MSPI_TIMING_FLASH_TEST_DATA_ADDR for each candidate config and picks the best passing one, logging a warning and falling back if none pass. Flash and PSRAM sit on independent MSPI controllers, so PSRAM's 250 MHz octal setting is untouched.
evidence: /opt/esp-idf/components/esp_hw_support/mspi/mspi_timing_tuning/port/esp32s31/mspi_timing_config.c — mspi_timing_config_set_flash_clock() under `#if MSPI_TIMING_FLASH_NEEDS_TUNING` with `assert(core_clock_mhz == 120)` and mspi_timing_ll_set_flash_core_clock(..., 120).

Same directory, mspi_timing_tuning_configs.h: `#else //CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHFREQ_120M` → `#define MSPI_TIMING_FLASH_MODULE_CLOCK 120`, `#define MSPI_TIMING_FLASH_NEEDS_TUNING (MSPI_TIMING_FLASH_MODULE_CLOCK > 80)`, `MSPI_TIMING_SPLL_FREQ_MHZ 480`, and `MSPI_TIMING_MSPI1_IS_INVOLVED CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHFREQ_120M`.

/opt/esp-idf/components/spi_flash/esp32s31/Kconfig.flash_freq offers only ESPTOOLPY_FLASHFREQ_80M/40M/20M — the only reason 120M cannot be selected today. esptool_py/Kconfig.projbuild already maps `default '80m' if ESPTOOLPY_FLASHFREQ_120M` (header stays 80m, software re-clocks after boot).

The missing table exists verbatim on three sibling targets: port/esp32p4/mspi_timing_tuning_configs.h:79-81, port/esp32c61:133-135, port/esp32c5:134-136, all `{{2,0,1},{0,0,0},{2,2,2},...}` with 12 entries.

soc_caps.h has SOC_SPI_MEM_SUPPORT_TIMING_TUNING and SOC_MEMSPI_TIMING_TUNING_BY_DQS, and SOC_PSRAM_MEMSPI_IS_INDEPENDENT / SOC_MEMSPI_IS_INDEPENDENT (flash and PSRAM clocks are separate). No SOC_SPI_MEM_FLASH_SUPPORT_HPM cap, so no high-performance-mode dummy-cycle dance is required.
docs/example_boot_log.txt:15-16,70 — 'SPI Speed : 80MHz', 'SPI Mode : QIO', 'detected chip: generic', 16 MB. Dead end #26 measured 22-32 MB/s at QIO-80.
magnitude_estimate: ~1.5x on flash read rate, i.e. a 64 B line fill from ~2 us to ~1.33 us, applied to every miss against 4.38 MB of kernel text plus the whole XIP userspace (Xorg/lvdesk/musl/SDL). It does not help code that already fits the 16 KB I-cache (footprintbench showed a 322 B loop is equal in flash and RAM), so the beneficiaries are the same paths .text..fast targets, plus boot and cold first-touch. Guess: low single digits on Quake, larger on SD/kernel-heavy and boot-time work. Cheaper than any relocation because it costs no RAM.
rule_check: No application rebuilt, relinked or steered. Apps stay on SD. Nothing disabled. Upstream is not patched in the forbidden sense — the edit is a Kconfig option and a timing table in the vendor firmware SDK we already build the loader from, not Xorg/mesa/dwc2. Zero RAM cost. DANGER worth stating: a marginal flash timing point corrupts XIP reads silently, and both the kernel and the XIP rootfs live there, so it needs a long read-back verification (checksum the whole xip window) and the tuning log captured before it is believed.
prior_attempts: Dead end #26: 'Flash mode/clock as a lever — Harvested. DIO -> QIO gave SD 4k -46% and CoreMark +17%. Flash is already QIO-80 (22-32 MB/s measured). 80 MHz is the S31 IDF maximum, with no timing-tuning port. OPI/DTR need other silicon.' The stated cause has since been fixed: the container's /opt/esp-idf (v6.1-dev) does ship components/esp_hw_support/mspi/mspi_timing_tuning/port/esp32s31 with the 120 MHz clock path implemented. OPI/DTR remain impossible; this is STR QIO at a higher clock, which is a different claim.

title: Give the CPU cache-refill master a real AXI QoS priority — all six interconnect masters ship at QoS 0
layer: hart0 loader, or a Linux runtime knob (the registers are in the ordinary peripheral aperture)
mechanism: The S31 system interconnect has a QoS arbiter with a 4-bit read and a 4-bit write priority per master: cpu, cache, dma2d, axi_pdma (AXI-GDMA), gmac and axi_sdmmc. Every field's documented reset value is 0 and nothing in ESP-IDF programs them — the only users of axi_icm_ll.h are the APM exception handlers and two unrelated chips' bootloader resets. So the port that services I-cache and D-cache line fills from PSRAM and flash arbitrates flat against the LCD scanout DMA (45.3 MB/s continuous at 59 Hz), the SD DMA, the PPA/2D-DMA and the radios' DMA. On a machine whose binding constraint is memory and whose CPU is documented as sitting at ~23% of its theoretical rate at idle, giving the cache master a higher read QoS than the streaming engines is the one-register version of 'stop making the CPU queue behind the display'. Registers: ICM_MST_ARQOS_REG0 at 0x20510428 (cpu [3:0], cache [7:4], dma2d [11:8], axi_pdma [15:12], gmac [19:16], axi_sdmmc [23:20]) and ICM_MST_AWQOS_REG0 at 0x20510430; ICM_CLK_EN at 0x20510404.
evidence: /opt/esp-idf/components/soc/esp32s31/register/soc/icm_sys_reg.h:41-82 — every *_ARQOS field is 'R/W; bitpos: [..]; default: 0'; same for the AWQOS register at +0x30.

/opt/esp-idf/components/hal/esp32s31/include/hal/axi_icm_ll.h — six setters (dma2d, gdma, gmac, sdmmc, cache, cpu). A grep for axi_icm_ll/ICM_SYS across all of IDF finds only apm_hal.c (interrupt/exception info) and the C5/C61 bootloaders' reset call; no target programs QoS.

reg_base.h:69 DR_REG_ICM_BASE 0x20510400, inside SOC_PERIPHERAL_LOW..HIGH (0x20100000..0x2E000000), i.e. reachable from Linux the same way the other S31 peripheral drivers reach theirs — so it can be a runtime toggle rather than a rebuild per hypothesis.

Dead end #12 measured the scanout load precisely: 59/50/42/35 Hz = 45.3/38.4/32.3/26.9 MB/s. Lowering the refresh rate changed nothing, which is consistent with a bandwidth-sharing problem that is about arbitration/latency rather than raw throughput.
magnitude_estimate: Unknown — this is a latency/arbitration knob, and the honest expectation is single digits, possibly zero. It is worth doing because it is a handful of register writes with a runtime toggle, it has never been touched, and it is the only lever that changes who wins when the CPU and the display DMA want PSRAM in the same cycle. Sweep it as a graded set (e.g. cache 8, cpu 8, dma2d/pdma 4, sdmmc 4) rather than cache=15, and watch for scanout underruns ('scanout started' geometry changes and 'no scanout buffer' lines) as the failure signal.
rule_check: No application touched. Apps stay on SD. Nothing disabled — this reprioritises, it does not switch anything off (so Bluetooth/Wi-Fi DMA keeps working; give the radios a non-zero QoS too). No upstream patching. Zero RAM.
prior_attempts: Not in the dead-end register and not in docs/. Distinct from dead end #11 (GDMA for the damage copy) and #34 (SD bus tuning), both of which changed who does the work rather than who wins the bus.

title: A `.text..sram` above `.text..fast`: put the very hottest kernel code in internal HP SRAM, where OpenSBI already gets 2.75x
layer: kernel linker script + OpenSBI/loader memory map (shared/s31_memory_layout.h)
mechanism: Internal HP SRAM sits in front of no cache at all, so code fetched from it pays neither the flash penalty nor the PSRAM penalty nor any I-cache/D-cache capacity. The project has already proved this on hart1: moving OpenSBI's trap dispatch into a 16 KiB SRAM window took the context switch 280.7 us to 57.2 us and SD 4k p50 3.79 to 2.21 ms, and the first 4,976 bytes of it alone (sbi_trap.o, sbi_ecall.o, esp32s31.o) took the switch 157.5 to 80.0 us. That is ~2x per 5 KB, far better per byte than .text..fast in PSRAM. There is free SRAM today: the memory-layout header records 9,216 bytes unallocated above S31_OPENSBI_FAST_END (0x2F07DC00..0x2F080000), and dead end #89 records a further 6,360 bytes unused inside the 16 KiB OpenSBI window — ~15 KB at zero cost, enough for the syscall/IRQ entry stub and the CLIC dispatch. Beyond that, the funding mechanism nobody has tried is to move hart0's heap into a PSRAM carve-out: hart0 is confined to internal SRAM purely by CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MEMMAP (PSRAM is mapped, never heap-managed) even though SOC_PSRAM_DMA_CAPABLE=1, so its ~196 KB heap is a policy choice, not a hardware one. Trading N KB of hart0 heap for N KB of PSRAM is roughly RAM-neutral for Linux once the corresponding .text..fast bytes are returned to PSRAM.
evidence: /Users/gadyke/esp32-s31-linux/shared/s31_memory_layout.h, S31_OPENSBI_FAST_BASE block: '16 KiB here ... 25,600 bytes are free between S31_HP_SHARED_END and the top of HP SRAM at 0x2F080000, so this leaves 9,216 spare' and 'the dispatch (sbi_trap.o, sbi_ecall.o, esp32s31.o - 4,976 bytes, which alone took the context switch 157.5 -> 80.0 us)'.

Dead end #37: 'OpenSBI trap path into internal SRAM — SRAM shipped: context switch 280.7 -> 57.2 us, SD 4k p50 3.79 -> 2.21 ms. PSRAM does not boot (hart1 M-mode cannot fetch from it).' Instruction fetch from internal SRAM by hart1 is therefore already proven in production.
bootloader/build/hello_world.map: sram_seg 0x2f000000 length 0x7afc0; _bss_end 0x2f031ea8, _heap_start 0x2f031eb0 — 204,464 B static, ~196 KB of heap below the 0x2F062000 reservation line.
bootloader/sdkconfig: CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MEMMAP=y, CONFIG_SPIRAM=y, CONFIG_SPIRAM_MODE_OCT=y, CONFIG_SPIRAM_SPEED_250M=y — PSRAM is mapped but not in hart0's heap. soc_caps.h: SOC_PSRAM_DMA_CAPABLE 1.

The kernel-side machinery already exists: patches/0028 and the .text..fast section work, and s31-textfast-textmain-trap records the linker glob hazard (use `.text..sram`, verify in System.map, never `.text.sram`).
magnitude_estimate: The free 15 KB is a small, cheap first arm: by the OpenSBI curve, ~5 KB of the hottest dispatch is worth roughly 2x on the path it sits on, so the target is the kernel trap/syscall entry and CLIC dispatch — which is precisely the code that FAILED to relocate into PSRAM (.text..fast irq spine did not boot, CLIC driver in RAM floods 'cause: 7'). Going to 64-128 KB by moving hart0's heap to PSRAM would put a real slice of the kernel at zero fetch cost; the .text..fast experience (softirq.o alone -19.7% on syscall/IPC round trips) suggests that is the same class of win, with better bytes.
rule_check: No application code touched; apps stay on SD and continue to page from it. Nothing disabled. No upstream patching — kernel linker script plus our own loader/OpenSBI map. RAM-neutral in the large version (PSRAM given to hart0 is offset by .text..fast bytes returned); the 15 KB first arm is free. Hazards to respect: internal SRAM needs an executable kernel mapping and PMA/PMP cover (the trampoline only sets PMA entry 7 for PSRAM today), and hart0 heap allocations moved to PSRAM would newly consume the shared 64 KB D-cache, which must be measured not assumed.
prior_attempts: Dead end #89 closes the general case — 'bigger I-cache, L2, TCM, whole kernel in RAM, 64 KB SRAM hot-text window ... the hart0 heap is 4-12 KiB free, so the only free SRAM is 6,360 B in the OpenSBI window.' That is an observation of the current allocation, not a hardware limit, and it misses both the 9,216 bytes the memory-layout header records above the OpenSBI window and the fact that hart0's confinement to SRAM is a single sdkconfig choice. Dead ends #56 and #57 are about PSRAM .text..fast, a different (and measurably worse) target memory.

title: Use the I-cache prelock that is already written into the kernel and has never been measured
layer: linux-71-port/drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c (prelock/preload) + kernel command line
mechanism: The L1 caches cannot be enlarged (every CACHESIZE and BLOCKSIZE field is marked HRO in cache_reg.h), but each I-cache has two prelock sections that pin an address range so it is never evicted, plus a preload engine that fills it without waiting for first execution. The driver in this tree already implements both against I-cache 1 — esp32s31_icache_prelock() programs PRELOCK_CONF/SCT0_ADDR/SCT1_ADDR/SCT_SIZE and then runs PRELOAD_CTRL to completion. The catch is that it is exposed only through debugfs, and the shipping kernel is built DIAG=0 because debugfs costs 1.14 MB of RAM, so the knob does not exist in any build anyone measures with. Turn it into a boot parameter (two `addr,size` pairs), lock the hottest 2-4 KB of the kernel entry path in its flash-window address, and the syscall/IRQ front door stops refetching from flash — without spending a byte of PSRAM and without the relocation hazards that killed the .text..fast IRQ-spine arms.
evidence: /Users/gadyke/esp32-s31-linux/linux-71-port/drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c: ESP32S31_ICACHE1_PRELOCK_CONF 0x04c, SCT0_ADDR 0x050, SCT1_ADDR 0x054, SCT_SIZE 0x058, PRELOAD_CTRL 0x0b8/ADDR 0x0bc/SIZE 0x0c0, with esp32s31_icache_prelock() and an esp32s31_prelock_write() debugfs handler. Its own comment: 'the 16 KiB I-cache cannot be enlarged. What *is* writable is which lines stay in it ... Code that stays resident never pays a fetch again.'
The same file notes 'the CPU is memory-bound even at idle (~23% of its theoretical rate with nothing else running)'.
grep -rniE 'prelock' over docs/, rootfs/, scripts/ and arch/riscv returns nothing — the feature was written and never written up, and it is not in the 98-entry dead-end register.
s31-debugfs-costs-ram: debugfs costs 1.14 MB even unmounted; DIAG=0 is the default build, so the debugfs-only interface is absent from every shipping kernel.

cache_reg.h: CACHE_L1_ICACHE_BLOCKSIZE_* and CACHE_L1_ICACHE_CACHESIZE_* are all 'HRO' with a 'for internal debugging purposes' note — confirming dead end #95 and ruling out resizing as an alternative.
magnitude_estimate: Bounded by how much can be pinned: the I-cache is 16 KB, 2-way, 128 sets, so locking 8 KB leaves the rest direct-mapped. The useful window is probably 1-4 KB — the trap entry plus CLIC dispatch. On the evidence that a 5 KB SRAM-resident dispatch halved OpenSBI's context switch, a permanently resident 2-4 KB entry path should be worth a comparable slice of syscall/IRQ cost, and the syscall/IPC round trip is the metric softirq.o moved 19.7%. Must be swept, because over-locking will cost more than it saves.
rule_check: No application touched. Apps stay on SD. Nothing disabled. No upstream patching — the driver is ours. Zero RAM cost, and removing the debugfs dependency actually saves the 1.14 MB that would otherwise be needed to use it. Note the addresses must be the flash-window bus addresses the cache sees (0x40xxxxxx), not kernel virtual addresses, and must be 64-byte aligned (the driver enforces the alignment).
prior_attempts: Absent from the dead-end register and from docs/. Dead end #89 dismissed 'bigger I-cache' as unavailable, which is true and is a different thing from controlling residency. Dead end #17 is the autoload/prefetch engine, a separate register block with a separate failure history.

title: The AXI performance monitor is a real PMU on a board documented as having none
layer: new Linux driver (or a loader-side dump) over AXI_PERF_MON at 0x20511000
mechanism: There is an on-chip bus performance monitor with seven agent slots, eight 32-bit metric counters per agent, per-counter metric selects, read and write address-region filters, AXI ID masks and filters, instantaneous-bandwidth tests with a time threshold and an under-limit interrupt, and 16-bit 'range' (interval) counters that a counter can run alongside its metric. The agents map to the same masters as the interconnect QoS register: cpu, cache, dma2d, axi_pdma, gmac, axi_sdmmc. That means it can answer, directly and without perturbing the workload, questions this project has repeatedly had to infer: how much PSRAM bandwidth the scanout DMA actually takes during a Quake demo, what fraction the cache-refill port gets, what the cache-refill latency distribution looks like, and whether a slow boot differs from a fast one on the bus. It is an instrument, not a speed-up — but every large win here was unlocked by an instrument (the hart0 PC sampler, the ioctl LD_PRELOAD timer, /proc/profile), and every large mistake was made without one.
evidence: /opt/esp-idf/components/soc/esp32s31/register/soc/axi_perf_mon_reg.h: AGENT_SELECT at +0x4 ('Select Agent in slot to be monitored, 4 bits means one agent number'), SEL_AGn_COUNTER0..7_RESULT, SEL_AGn_RANGE0.. ('The interval statistics results in this counter'), and METRIC_SELECT0/1/2 ('each agent use 8 bits, low 5 bits means which metric is selected for current counter, high 3 bits means range metric this counter measured, a counter can use metric and range measure at the same time').

title: Pin the MSPI/PSRAM timing point across boots — it is re-derived every boot, chosen at the edge of the passing window, and never logged
layer: hart0 loader (ESP-IDF MSPI timing tuning) / boot instrumentation
mechanism: PSRAM at 250 MHz octal requires DQS timing tuning, which the loader performs on every cold boot ('Enter psram timing tuning' in the boot log). The routine sweeps four DQS phases and 31 delayline settings, finds the consecutive window of settings that read the reference pattern correctly, and picks a point in it. For the delayline it picks the midpoint (`end - consecutive_length/2`); for the phase it picks the FIRST element of the window (`end - consecutive_length + 1`), i.e. the edge. The result is stored in statics and logged only at DEBUG, so nobody has ever seen which point a given boot chose. On a machine whose binding constraint is memory, a per-boot difference in PSRAM read timing is exactly the shape of the unexplained ±10% per-boot Quake lottery — and the project has already measured, and then set aside, a 274.8 vs 316 ns spread in PSRAM chase latency between boots. Chase latency is a dependent-load metric; the machine is streaming-bound, so a correlation failing on chase latency does not clear per-boot memory timing. Step 1 is free: raise the MSPI Timing log level for one boot in each of several boots and record phase + delayline alongside the timedemo. Step 2, if they vary: force the recorded best point (and take the midpoint of the phase window rather than its edge).
evidence: /opt/esp-idf/components/esp_hw_support/mspi/mspi_timing_tuning/tuning_scheme_impl/mspi_timing_by_dqs.c:132-151 — mspi_timing_psram_select_best_tuning_phase() returns `(end - consecutive_length + 1)`; :190-203 — mspi_timing_psram_select_best_tuning_delayline() returns `end - consecutive_length / 2`. Both log only via ESP_DRAM_LOGD.

Same file:114-120 — only four phases are available (67.5, 78.75, 90, 101.25 degrees); :54-57 — a 31-entry delayline table. s_psram_best_phase / s_psram_best_delayline are file statics, recomputed each boot.

port/esp32s31/mspi_timing_tuning_configs.h: `#if CONFIG_SPIRAM_SPEED_250M → MSPI_TIMING_PSRAM_NEEDS_TUNING 1, MSPI_TIMING_MPLL_FREQ_MHZ 500`; bootloader/sdkconfig has CONFIG_SPIRAM_SPEED_250M=y, CONFIG_SPIRAM_MODE_OCT=y.
docs/example_boot_log.txt:48 — 'I (219) MSPI Timing: Enter psram timing tuning' on every boot.

Dead end #70: 'Not PSRAM chase latency (a slow boot at 274.8 ns, fast boots at 316 ns).' A 15% per-boot spread in PSRAM latency is itself the finding; it was used to dismiss a hypothesis rather than investigated. The lottery's cause is still recorded as unknown.
magnitude_estimate: If a marginal phase is part of the lottery, up to the lottery band itself (~10% on Quake, and far more valuable than that as measurement productivity — every A/B on this board currently needs 3-4 fresh boots per arm to see past it). If the tuned point turns out identical on every boot, the cost is one log-level change and the hypothesis is closed with evidence, which the register currently lacks.
rule_check: No application touched. Apps stay on SD. Nothing disabled. No upstream patching in the forbidden sense — a log level, then at most a pinned constant in the vendor firmware SDK we already build. Zero RAM. Pinning a timing point is a flash-state change in the loader, so it belongs in the 'record any flash state you write' note; it is reverted by reflashing the loader.
prior_attempts: Dead end #70 lists the lottery eliminations: not placement, not an lvdesk restart, not the scanout buffer, not CMA, not PSRAM chase latency, not cpu1_busy, not Quake paging. The MSPI tuning point is not among them, and the chase-latency entry is the closest anyone has come.

title: Switch swap-in to physical-slot readahead (vma_ra_enabled=0) and raise page-cluster — the one swap-readahead mode this board has never run
layer: kernel mm / sysctl+sysfs policy (no rebuild)
mechanism:
Every major fault today is one 4 KB SD request. mm/swap_state.c:44 sets `enable_vma_readahead = true`, and mm/swapfile.c:3563 gives the mmc-backed swapfile SWP_SOLIDSTATE (mmc never sets BLK_FEAT_ROTATIONAL), so `swap_use_vma_readahead()` (mm/swap_state.c:409) is TRUE and `swapin_readahead()` (mm/swap_state.c:899-901) always takes the VMA branch. With vm.page-cluster=0 the VMA window is 1, so no readahead happens at all — 1,296 separate 2.49 ms requests per Quake demo.

The untried mode is `echo 0 > /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled` + vm.page-cluster=2 or 3. That selects `swap_cluster_readahead()`, which reads N pages around the faulting page's *swap slot*, not its virtual address. Slot allocation is per-cpu sequential within a cluster, and reclaim walks the LRU in order, so pages evicted together get adjacent slots. Those N reads issue under one blk_plug and the block layer merges them into ONE request: at page-cluster=3, 32 KB costs 2.49 + 32/48000 s = 3.16 ms against 8 x 2.58 = 20.6 ms as singles — 6.5x fewer milliseconds per 8 pages actually wanted.

This is precisely why the recorded page-cluster experiments failed: they all ran in VMA mode, where 8 virtually-adjacent pages live in 8 scattered slots, so clustering multiplies requests instead of merging them. 99-s31-memory.conf even argues the mechanism correctly ("swapped-out anonymous pages are not laid out the way a sequential read is") — that is true of virtual order and false of slot order.
evidence: linux-71-port/mm/swap_state.c:44,409,899-901 — enable_vma_readahead defaults true; dispatch to swap_vma_readahead vs swap_cluster_readahead
linux-71-port/mm/swapfile.c:3563-3568 — !bdev_rot() ⇒ SWP_SOLIDSTATE, nr_rotate_swap stays 0, so VMA mode is the live mode for /swapfile on mmcblk

CLAUDE.md measured constant: SD request = 2.49 ms + size/48 MB/s, flat ~2.0 ms floor below 16 KiB
dead-ends.json #33 states in its own result field: "Physical-slot mode (vma_ra_enabled=0) has never been tried."
magnitude_estimate: If half the clustered pages are wanted, the ~1,296 swap requests collapse to ~300-400 merged 16-32 KB requests: 3.3 s of SD wall time becomes ~1.0-1.3 s, i.e. ~2-2.5 s off a 58.5 s demo = +3.5-4.5% fps (16.6 → ~17.3-17.4), and a disproportionately larger cut to the frame-time tail because a readahead hit turns a 2.6 ms blocking fault into a microsecond swap-cache minor fault. Also applies to desktop app-launch latency, which is the original complaint class. Upside if slot locality is good: 2-3x fewer requests still.
rule_check: PASSES. Two runtime knobs (/sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled, vm.page-cluster) — no app rebuilt, relinked, wrapped or config-steered; apps stay on SD; nothing disabled; no upstream code patched; zero permanent RAM cost (readahead pages are reclaimable). Risk to name: with MemAvailable ~1.3 MB, an 8-page window adds allocation pressure, so start at page-cluster=2 (4 pages, 2.82 ms vs 10.3 ms) before 3.
prior_attempts: dead-ends.json #33 and #66 record page-cluster 3 and 5 as measured-and-rejected (Xorg era 201.1/198.8/203.5 CoreMark; Quake at 48 kHz "did not finish in 170 s vs 167 s"). Every one of those arms ran with vma_ra_enabled at its default 1, which is a different algorithm — the register itself carves the physical-slot mode out as untried. #19 (swappiness=0) and #1 (zram) are unrelated. Must be measured with fresh boot per arm and the shipped s31route_11k audio device, per the ±10% Quake per-boot lottery (docs/smp-finish-plan.md).

title: zswap with writeback at a small pool cap — the compressed-swap shape that zram structurally could not provide
layer: kernel config (mm) + runtime module parameters
mechanism:
CONFIG_ZSWAP is absent from the build (confirmed by grep over /src/build/linux/.config), while everything it needs is already there: CONFIG_ZSMALLOC=y, CONFIG_ZRAM_BACKEND_LZO=y, and mm/Kconfig's ZSWAP depends only on SWAP and selects CRYPTO + ZSMALLOC. So the incremental image cost is roughly zswap.o + zpool glue against 119,803 bytes of linux-partition slack.

zram was rejected here for one recorded structural reason: a capped zram device "can never fall through: at the limit it returns -ENOMEM and the folio is re-dirtied" (zram_drv.c:2241-2243), so the pool had to be sized to hold everything and grew to 2.8-3.2 MB, buying compression by taking residency. zswap inverts that: it is a *cache in front of* the existing /swapfile. When the pool hits zswap.max_pool_percent it writes its LRU entries back to the SD swapfile and accepts the new page, so a deliberately small cap is a valid configuration rather than a failure mode. zswap.shrinker_enabled additionally writes back proactively under pressure.

Concretely: zswap.max_pool_percent=5-8 (≈770 kB-1.2 MB of 15.4 MB) holding ~2-3 MB of Quake's 6.2-7.4 MB VmSwap. A hit is an lzo-rle decompress of 4 KB (tens of microseconds at this core's 102 MB/s PSRAM copy rate) instead of a 2.58 ms SD request — 20-35x. Because the pool holds pages that are *already evicted*, a 1 MB pool covering 2.5 MB of swapped anon is net memory-positive relative to leaving them on the card. Every parameter is under /sys/module/zswap/parameters, so the pool size and enable flag A/B on a warm board with no reflash — the project's preferred "runtime toggle over rebuild-per-hypothesis" style.
evidence: linux-71-port/mm/Kconfig — config ZSWAP depends on SWAP; select CRYPTO, ZSMALLOC (both already built)
Built .config (container grep): CONFIG_ZSWAP absent; CONFIG_ZSMALLOC=y, CONFIG_ZRAM_BACKEND_LZO=y, CONFIG_ZRAM_DEF_COMP="lzo-rle"
dead-ends.json #1 — the zram verdict's stated cause is the no-fall-through property (zram_drv.c:2241-2243) plus a 2.8-3.2 MB pool costing residency; neither applies to a writeback-capable cache

MEASURED CONSTANTS: SD request 2.49 ms + size/48 MB/s; PSRAM copy 102 MB/s
magnitude_estimate: At a 1 MB cap holding ~2.5 MB of a 6.2 MB swapped set with LRU ordering, expect 30-50% of the 1,296 major faults served from RAM: ~500 faults x 2.5 ms = ~1.2 s off a 58.5 s demo ≈ +2% fps, plus a much better tail (the 50-100 ms frame bucket). Larger on the desktop/app-launch path, where the complaint is latency not throughput. Downside bounded and reversible: the cap is a runtime knob, and unlike zram the overflow path is a write-back rather than an -ENOMEM.
rule_check: PASSES. Kernel config + module parameters only; no app touched; apps stay on SD; nothing disabled; no upstream code patched. The one real tension is the 15.3-15.4 MB constraint — this spends RAM — which is why the proposal is a *small, runtime-tunable* cap with automatic fall-through, and why the arm must report MemAvailable and Quake RssAnon alongside fps.
prior_attempts: dead-ends.json #1 closes zram in every form tried (24 MB / 4 MB / 512 kB mem_limit, Weston/X/lvdesk eras) and #40 notes zero-folio handling is already free in 7.1's swap zeromap. zswap has never been built here. Adjacent closure worth recording: MGLRU is not merely untested but unavailable — dead-ends #39 flags "the FLATMEM route (C54) is untested", but arch/riscv/Kconfig:1326 makes XIP_KERNEL depend on SPARSEMEM (flash text and rodata must have no memmap), so FLATMEM cannot be selected and LRU_GEN's `64BIT || !SPARSEMEM || SPARSEMEM_VMEMMAP` can never be satisfied on this board. That route is closed, not open.

title: Function-granular .text..fast: 285 kB of RAM is spent on hot-text relocation and 77% of it never executes
layer: kernel build flags + our own XIP linker script
mechanism:
`.text..fast` is placed by whole-object globs (`*sched/fair.o`, `*workqueue.o`, `*blk-core.o`...). Measuring the region against the board's own Quake profile: __text_fast_start c083bc50 .. __text_fast_end c0881990 = 285,534 bytes containing 3,184 symbols, of which only 296 (66,992 B, 23%) took a single PC sample in 12,000, and only 155 (45,658 B, 16%) took three or more. Roughly 215-240 kB of the most expensive memory on the board is holding error paths, ioctl arms, setup code and rarely-taken branches that happen to share an object file with something hot.

Compiling with `-ffunction-sections` (CONFIG_HAVE_LD_DEAD_CODE_DATA_ELIMINATION=y on riscv with GNU ld; CONFIG_FUNCTION_ALIGNMENT=0, so per-function padding is negligible) makes placement per function instead of per object. Two payoffs:

(a) Return ~200 kB of RAM at unchanged speed — 1.3% of total memory, and roughly 15% of a typical MemAvailable of ~1.3 MB — straight into the constraint that the whole board is bound by.

(b) Make the hot code still in flash affordable. The top 120 flash-resident symbols outside idle carry 14.0% of ALL CPU0 samples in 38.4 kB of code; the generic IRQ dispatch chain alone (esp32s31_clic_handle_irq, handle_percpu_devid_irq, __irq_resolve_mapping, handle_irq_desc, generic_handle_domain_irq, handle_level_irq, __handle_irq_event_percpu, note_interrupt, call_on_irq_stack, handle_exception, ret_from_exception) is 554 samples = 4.6% in 5.0 kB. As whole objects those are the 24-43 kB batches that were measured and reverted for costing more D-cache than they bought; at function granularity they are single-digit kB.

Plumbing: the script already solves the hard part — it redefines TEXT_TEXT/SCHED_TEXT/LOCK_TEXT/NOINSTR_TEXT with EXCLUDE_FILE so the flash `.text` does not claim the fast objects first, and the documented two-dot `.text..fast` name is invisible to TEXT_MAIN's globs. EXCLUDE_FILE is per-file, so function granularity needs one of two routes: place the `.text..fast` output section before `.text` in the script with an explicit address, or add an objcopy `--rename-section .text.<fn>=.text..fastfn` pass over the chosen functions and glob `*(.text..fastfn)` — the two-dot name that TEXT_MAIN provably cannot match. KCFLAGS is already set from our Makefile (Makefile:650), so no upstream source is edited.

Bonus with CONFIG_LD_DEAD_CODE_DATA_ELIMINATION=y (currently "not set" though HAVE_ is y): --gc-sections typically returns 3-6% of image size, which would more than repay the 119,803 B of remaining linux-partition slack that killed whole-kernel -O2.

Same profile, flash-resident and excluding arch_cpu_idle: top 120 symbols = 1,678 samples (14.0% of all) in 38,400 B; IRQ-dispatch subset = 554 samples (4.6%) in 5,002 B

magnitude_estimate: Primary, high-confidence: ~200 kB of RAM returned with no speed loss (measured from the project's own profile + System.map). On a board where Quake has 6.2 MB swapped and MemAvailable sits ~1.3 MB, that is ~50 fewer swapped pages and ~15% more MemAvailable. Secondary, medium-confidence: adding the 14%-of-samples flash hot set at ~35-40 kB instead of the 200+ kB it would cost as whole objects; by the softirq.o precedent (-19.7% on a pingpong round trip for one object) the IRQ-dispatch 5 kB is the single best-value candidate left. Combined, this is the lever that unblocks the second-biggest past win rather than replacing it.
rule_check: PASSES. Build flags and our own linker script; no application rebuilt, relinked or steered; apps stay on SD and this gives them more RAM; nothing disabled; no upstream source edited (KCFLAGS comes from our Makefile, the .lds.S is already a local file). Watch: -ffunction-sections without --gc-sections adds section padding against 119,803 B of slack — the build already fails loudly on overflow (Makefile:655-667), and enabling DCE gives the slack back. Every relocation must be verified in System.map per the s31-textfast-textmain-trap rule.
prior_attempts: dead-ends #0, #25, #55, #56, #57 all concern moving WHOLE OBJECTS into RAM and are largely negative for exactly the reason measured here — reclaim 33/97 kB no effect; the 43 kB profiled batch #320 an A/B/A-confirmed 5% regression; rcu/tree.o 24 kB for -1.7%; SMP objects 15.75 → 15.79; DRM commit 26.8 kB inside noise. #89 closes "whole kernel in RAM" on size. None of them tried function granularity, and the register's own stated conclusion ("pick by how often EXECUTED") is unreachable at object granularity. Bootstrap exclusions still apply and must be kept: memcpy/memset/memmove, time/sched_clock.o, arch_sync_dma_for_device, locking/spinlock.o.

title: HRTICK became a default-on scheduler feature in 7.1, and on this hart every hrtimer reprogram is an SBI ecall into M-mode
layer: kernel config / scheduler feature defaults
mechanism:
linux-71-port/kernel/sched/features.h:68-73 sets SCHED_FEAT(HRTICK, true) and SCHED_FEAT(HRTICK_DL, true) whenever CONFIG_HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED is y. In linux-70-port and linux-618-port the same lines read `false` unconditionally — this is a 7.1-only change of default. riscv selects GENERIC_ENTRY (arch/riscv/Kconfig:111) and HAVE_GENERIC_TIF_BITS (:167), and the build has HIGH_RES_TIMERS=y and SCHED_HRTICK=y, so kernel/time/Kconfig:58-61's `def_bool y` fires: the shipping kernel confirms CONFIG_HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED=y. HRTICK is therefore ON, and with no CONFIG_SCHED_DEBUG the feature is compile-time — there is no runtime knob and nobody has looked at it.

What that costs here specifically: HRTICK arms a per-rq hrtimer at the running task's virtual deadline on every pick/enqueue/dequeue where more than one task is queued (kernel/sched/fair.c:7040-7089), and cancels it on the way out. Each arm/cancel reprograms the clockevent. This hart's ISA string (rv32imafc_zicntr_zicsr_zifencei_zca_zcf_zba_zbb_zbc_zbs) has no `sstc`, so drivers/clocksource/timer-riscv.c:52-61 takes the fallback branch: `sbi_set_timer()` — an ecall trap into M-mode OpenSBI — for every single reprogram. Upstream's cost model for HRTICK is a local APIC write; ours is a privilege transition. HRTICK_DL does the same for the fair deadline server that 6.12+ runs on every CPU.

The board already shows the symptom: /proc/timer_list under Quake lists `hrtick` and `dl_task_timer` as live timers, and CPU0 takes ~227 timer interrupts/s at HZ=100 — 127/s that the periodic tick does not explain — while timers/clock account for 4.8% of CPU0 PC samples and M-mode for 1%.

First arm is a pure kconfig-tweak (`--disable HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED`), which flips both features off with no source edit. If it wins, split the two effects with a one-line patch in patches/ that keeps deferred rearm and forces HRTICK/HRTICK_DL false — the same mechanism as patches/0056 and 0057. Measure with rootfs/pingpong same-hart medians over 3 fresh boots (the harness the softirq.o result was established on), not the Quake lottery, and confirm the mechanism by counting the RISC-V timer line in /proc/interrupts before and after.
evidence: linux-71-port/kernel/sched/features.h:68-73 — HRTICK/HRTICK_DL true under CONFIG_HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED; linux-70-port/kernel/sched/features.h:66-67 and linux-618-port/kernel/sched/features.h:66-67 both read false
linux-71-port/kernel/time/Kconfig:58-61 — HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED def_bool y on GENERIC_ENTRY && HAVE_GENERIC_TIF_BITS && HIGH_RES_TIMERS && SCHED_HRTICK
Built .config (container grep): CONFIG_HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED=y, CONFIG_SCHED_HRTICK=y, CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS=y, CONFIG_GENERIC_ENTRY=y, CONFIG_HAVE_GENERIC_TIF_BITS=y, no CONFIG_SCHED_DEBUG
linux-71-port/drivers/clocksource/timer-riscv.c:38-61 — sbi_set_timer() fallback when SSTC is unavailable; CLAUDE.md's reported ISA string contains no sstc

linux-71-port/kernel/sched/fair.c:7040-7089 — hrtick_start_fair arms whenever rq->cfs.h_nr_queued > 1
magnitude_estimate: If hrtick accounts for a substantial share of the 127/s unexplained timer interrupts, removing it returns roughly 1-3% of CPU0 (timers are 4.8%, M-mode 1%) plus the per-switch arm/cancel that never shows as an interrupt. Quake's main thread is 84% of a core, so ~+1.5-2.5% fps; the effect should be several times larger on switch- and wakeup-heavy paths, which is where pingpong measures. Costs nothing: no RAM, slightly less text, one kconfig-tweak. Also a concrete, never-examined candidate for part of the unexplained 6.12→7.1 syscall regression recorded in memory note s31-generic-entry-cost (15.2 → 43.0 us for a read+write pair) — it cannot be all of it, since 7.0 also had HRTICK false, but it is on exactly that path and has never been isolated.
rule_check: PASSES. One kconfig-tweak in our Makefile for the first arm; optionally a one-line default flip carried in patches/ afterwards, which is the project's existing mechanism for kernel changes and is not Xorg/mesa/dwc2. No application rebuilt, relinked or steered; apps stay on SD; nothing disabled for speed; zero RAM. Risk to name: HRTICK exists to bound slice overrun, so latency-sensitive arms (input lag, the frame-gap histogram) should be reported alongside throughput, not just fps.
prior_attempts: Not in the dead-end register. #67 covers scheduler tunables (RUN_TO_PARITY, base_slice_ns, DELAY_DEQUEUE) and the preemption model, #32 covers HZ 250 vs 100, #68 covers NO_HZ_IDLE (which lost a timer wake and hangs) — none of them touches HRTICK, and the register's timer entries (#58 touch-poll/hw_vblank; #88 "systimer clocksource not running") are about device timers, not the scheduler's per-slice hrtimer. Note that hw_vblank=1 was already found inert, so the 127/s excess is not the LCD vblank tick.

title: The LCD controller interrupt fires 42-60x/s to increment three counters that the shipping kernel cannot read
layer: kernel / our DRM driver (esp32s31-lcd.c)
mechanism: esp32s31_lcd_pipe_enable() writes LCD_INT_MASK (VSYNC|TRANS_DONE|UNDERRUN) into LCD_DMA_INT_ENA_REG unconditionally (line 1778). esp32s31_lcd_irq() then does two readl()s (INT_ST, INT_RAW), one writel() to clear, updates five debug counters, and acts ONLY if the `hw_vblank` module parameter is set - which defaults to false and was measured inert. The counters it maintains (vsync_irqs, trans_done_irqs, underrun_irqs, dbg_irq_*) are read only by esp32s31_lcd_updates_show(), a debugfs seq_file, and debugfs is compiled out of the shipping kernel (DIAG=0). So on every shipped boot this is a hardware interrupt at the panel refresh rate whose entire effect is unreadable telemetry. title: Every device interrupt pays three CLIC MMIO writes and three spinlock+mmiowb pairs that protect nothing and mask nothing

title: HRTICK and HRTICK_DL are ON in this tree (upstream's default is off), and every clock-event reprogram is an SBI ecall because there is no Sstc

title: Critical-word-first and early restart are both at reset default 0 — every cache miss waits for the whole 64-byte line
layer: SoC cache controller (runtime-togglable from Linux; loader fallback)
mechanism: CACHE_L1_CACHE_WRAP_AROUND_CTRL_REG (0x2C000028) bit 1 = CACHE_L1_ICACHE1_WRAP and bit 4 = CACHE_L1_DCACHE_WRAP, both 'R/W, default: 0', documented as 'Configures whether to enable the critical word first function'. CACHE_L1_CACHE_MISS_ACCESS_CTRL_REG (0x2C00002C) bits 1 and 4 are 'R/W, default: 0', documented as 'Configures whether to enable early restart function'. The vendor cache chapter lists 'Critical word first and early restart' as features of this cache. IDF exposes these as Kconfig options on S2/S3/C2 and has no S31 Kconfig at all, so nothing in the loader or ESP-IDF ever sets them — the board is running with both off. With them off, an I-cache miss on XIP flash stalls the hart until all 64 bytes land; with them on it restarts at the requested word. This is a two-bit write that applies to all 4.38 MB of flash-resident kernel text and to every PSRAM data miss, i.e. it is not object-granular like .text..fast. Test as a runtime toggle from Linux (the register is plainly R/W and hart1 owns ICACHE1), flipping it from PSRAM-resident code, with proposal 1's counters and a code-fetch microbenchmark either side.

magnitude_estimate: Unknown but structurally broad. A 64 B line at the measured 22-32 MB/s flash rate is ~2.0-2.9 us of transfer; early restart converts the average wait from a whole line to roughly one beat. Against a kernel where moving one 10 kB object (softirq.o) out of flash was worth -19.7% on a syscall round trip, a global reduction in miss stall is plausibly several percent end-to-end. Risk: wrapped bursts may need MSPI/flash/PSRAM support that S31's soc_caps does not claim — early restart (0x2c) is the safer half and does not need wrapped bursts. Read the two registers first (free, devmem), then toggle one bit at a time with a rollback image staged.
rule_check: Platform-side register write only. No app touched, apps stay on SD, nothing disabled, no upstream code patched, zero RAM.
prior_attempts: Not in the dead-end register. Distinct from dead-end 17 (I-cache autoload — a prefetch flag that is a no-op while the cache is on, and which killed the hart when poked from Linux; these are documented R/W policy bits, not a flag with a stated precondition) and from dead-end 26 (flash mode/clock, harvested at QIO-80). Dead-end 95 ('enlarge or reconfigure the caches') was answered on geometry (sizes are hardware read-only) and never considered fill policy.

title: I-cache prelock is already implemented in our kernel driver, has never been measured, and is sized against a cache size that the hardware contradicts
layer: Kernel — drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c (already written)
mechanism: esp32s31_icache_prelock() pins an address range into hart1's I-cache via ICACHE1_PRELOCK_CONF/SCT0/SCT1 and then fills it with the preload engine, exposed at /sys/kernel/debug/esp32s31_cache/icache_prelock. Pinning hot XIP kernel text costs ZERO RAM — unlike .text..fast, which spends the binding constraint and which has repeatedly failed to boot (the whole IRQ spine, sched_clock.o, spinlock.o, memcpy all produced no-boot arms). A locked line is never re-fetched from flash at all, so for the locked range it should be strictly better than .text..fast, which still misses the I-cache and refills from PSRAM. Two things block it from being a result today: (a) the knob is debugfs-only and CONFIG_DEBUG_FS is off in the shipping build, so it needs a module-param/sysfs path before it can ship; (b) the driver's own comment sizes it against '16 KiB I-cache' while CACHE_L1_ICACHE_CACHESIZE_CONF_REG reports CACHESIZE_32K default 1 and the vendor chapter says 32 KB — so a sweep planned on the 16 KB assumption would stop at half the real capacity. Drive the range selection from the /proc/profile buckets already collected (IRQ/CLIC/entry 6.4%, scheduler 5.1%, timers 4.8% of CPU0), sweep 2/4/8/16 KB per section, and read hit/miss/conflict from proposal 1 to see whether locking a way is costing the rest of the kernel more than it saves.

magnitude_estimate: The comparable measured point is softirq.o (~10 kB) in RAM = -19.7% on a syscall/IPC round trip, shipped. 8-16 kB of locked flash text should reach the same class of effect at zero RAM cost, and it composes with the existing .text..fast set rather than competing for the same budget. Downside risk is real and measurable: locking N bytes removes one of two ways over the locked set span, so the sweep must watch CONFLICT_CNT for the rest of the kernel.

prior_attempts: Dead-ends 25/55/56/57 are all about moving objects into RAM (.text..fast). None of them locks flash text in cache. title: Sv32 is completely unpriced on this board: the walker bypasses the D-cache, the linear map is all 4 KB pages, and every set_pte costs two hardware cache operations plus two ktime_get_ns
layer: Kernel mm / arch/riscv + our cache driver
mechanism: Three facts compound and none has ever been measured. (1) head.S states the S31 Sv32 walker does not snoop the shared write-back D-cache — so a TLB miss reads page tables straight out of PSRAM, at the ~275-316 ns random-access latency the lottery work already measured, twice per miss for a two-level walk, with no PTE caching and no spatial locality within a page-table page. (2) best_map_size() gates PMD_SIZE (4 MB) mappings on IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_64BIT), so on rv32 all 15.4 MB of linear map is 4 KB PTEs (~3,850 entries) even though Sv32 supports 4 MB megapages — every kernel-mode touch of the page cache, skbuffs and pixel buffers is a potential uncached two-level walk. (3) set_pte() calls esp32s31_cache_writeback() unconditionally, which routes into esp32s31_cache_range(): raw spinlock with IRQs off, ktime_get_ns() twice, three atomic64 RMWs, four MMIO writes, a busy-wait poll, then the whole hardware op issued a SECOND time for the writeback-class workaround with another poll, then a full mb() — for a 4-byte store, on every fault, COW, swap-in, swap-out, fork and unmap. The stats counters are not behind any CONFIG, so the shipping kernel pays for numbers it cannot read (CONFIG_DEBUG_FS is off), which is exactly the 'diagnostics left on control-flow paths' trap. INSTRUMENT: a userspace pointer-chase sweeping span at fixed touch count (stride 4 KB, N pages, one access each) finds the TLB entry count and the per-miss penalty in one run with no kernel change; a counter in esp32s31_cache_writeback gives set_pte/s during a Quake demo. LEVERS it unlocks, in order of cheapness: compile the stats out; batch or elide the PTE writeback (one op per pte range, not per PTE); megapage the linear map (a one-line change to a rv32 gate, 'it either boots or it does not'); and, if the walker is truly uncached, allocate page-table pages from the uncached PSRAM alias so set_pte needs no cache op at all.

title: The AXI performance monitor at 0x20511000 gives per-master bandwidth and latency histograms — the direct answer to 'is this memory-bound?', asked by arithmetic and got wrong before
layer: SoC bus fabric + a kernel driver of ours
mechanism: DR_REG_AXI_PERF_MON_BASE = 0x20511000 exposes 7 selectable agents x 8 programmable counters, each counter carrying min/max results, plus eight programmable latency RANGE buckets per agent (metric_range*_cnt_high/low), per-agent read and write bandwidth counters, instantaneous-bandwidth thresholds with interrupts, and — decisively — per-agent RD/WR address mask+filter registers, so traffic can be attributed to an address window (flash 0x40000000-0x4FFFFFFF vs PSRAM 0x50000000-0x53FFFFFF, or one buffer). That settles, with measurement rather than inference: how much of PSRAM's capability the machine actually uses under two harts; whether the 102 MB/s CPU copy is latency- or occupancy-bound; whether hart0's radio firmware fetching its own XIP text through the same flash controller is stealing bandwidth from hart1's kernel text while Wi-Fi/BT are live; and what fraction of bus latency lives in the tail rather than the mean. Bring-up cost: the agent-to-master mapping is not documented, so it has to be discovered empirically (drive a known GDMA transfer, see which agent moves) — budget a day for that before any result.

title: mcycle and minstret are already running and readable from S-mode — per-task IPC has never been measured once
layer: OpenSBI (already configured) + kernel context-switch accounting; one line in head.S for userspace
mechanism: OpenSBI writes mcounteren = -1 and mcountinhibit = 0xFFFFFFF8, which leaves bit 0 (CY) and bit 2 (IR) uninhibited and delegates both to S-mode. So the kernel can rdcycle/rdinstret today at essentially zero cost, on hart1. Accumulating both per task at __switch_to gives per-process instructions-retired and cycles, i.e. IPC, with the application binary untouched — which answers the question every PC-sample profile leaves open: Quake's 59% user-mode time is either executing or stalled, and the lever is codegen in one case and memory in the other. Nothing in this project has ever counted an instruction. Userspace visibility needs scounteren to gain CY|IR (head.S currently writes 0x2, TM only) — a one-line platform change that lets any tool self-measure without touching app code. Note also that drivers/perf/riscv_pmu_sbi.c has an explicit path for hpm_width == 0 using CSR_CYCLE/CSR_INSTRET, so a PROF=1 build could plausibly expose 'perf stat -e cycles,instructions' — worth an hour to check before building anything bespoke.

title: Settle the plus-or-minus-10% per-boot lottery with the hardware conflict counters and kill it with a prelock control
layer: Kernel — cache counters + physical page placement
mechanism: The 2026-09-21 investigation eliminated placement, lvdesk restart, scanout buffer address, CMA, PSRAM chase latency and Quake paging, and closed with the conclusion that what remains 'is state fixed at boot: physical memory placement, and specifically aliasing ... in a D-cache both harts share', and a stated next step — record the addresses per boot and correlate — that was never carried out. The addresses are the weak version of that experiment; the hardware has the strong version. The D-cache is 64 KB, 2-way, 64 B lines and is indexed by physical address (our own maintenance ops take phys_addr_t), so index bits are PA[14:6] and a 4 KB page carries 3 colour bits: eight colours, two ways, no page colouring anywhere in Linux on riscv. The I-cache is 2-way, 64 B lines and 16 or 32 KB, so 2-3 colour bits — and Quake's text pages arrive from SD into arbitrary physical frames every boot, so which of its hot render functions alias each other is literally re-rolled at each boot and then fixed for the run, which is exactly the observed signature (a reset leaves a slow boot slow because the layout is re-rolled, not because it is sticky). EXPERIMENT: per boot, log CONFLICT_CNT and MISS_CNT for IBUS1 and DBUS0/1 across the timedemo alongside the fps, n>=6 fresh boots; a monotone correlation identifies the cache and the axis in one run. DECISIVE CONTROL: pin the hot text with the prelock (proposal 3) — if the lottery collapses when the contended lines cannot be evicted, it was aliasing. FIX, if confirmed: colour-aware placement for the small hot objects on the platform side (our DRM buffers, lvdesk/xshim segments) or a colour-biased allocation path for the app's text pages — kernel work, app binary untouched.

title: Swap readahead in PHYSICAL-slot mode: the page-cluster sweeps were all run in VMA mode, where clustering multiplies requests instead of enlarging them
layer: kernel mm tuning (sysfs + sysctl), no code change
mechanism: Two independent swap readahead algorithms exist and `vm.page-cluster` feeds both. `swap_use_vma_readahead()` returns `enable_vma_readahead && !nr_rotate_swap` (mm/swap_state.c:407-409); the SD swapfile is non-rotational, so the board has ALWAYS been in VMA mode. `swap_vma_readahead()` walks PTEs around the faulting *virtual* address; the swap slots behind those PTEs are scattered, so N readahead pages become N separate bios that cannot merge — at page-cluster=3 that is up to 8 x 2.2 ms instead of 1 x 2.2 ms. That is exactly why every page-cluster sweep measured neutral-to-worse, and why 99-s31-memory.conf concluded 'the extra bytes are fetched and discarded'. `swap_cluster_readahead()` (mm/swap_state.c:697-745) is a different thing: it reads an ALIGNED PHYSICAL block of 1<<page_cluster slots inside one `blk_start_plug`/`blk_finish_plug`, so contiguous slots merge into ONE block request. Swap slots are handed out sequentially from per-CPU clusters as `shrink_folio_list` walks the LRU, so pages evicted together get adjacent slots — physical adjacency IS the temporal-locality predictor that VMA mode lacks here. The change is `echo 0 > /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled` plus `vm.page-cluster=2` (or 3). This is the direct application of the board's own documented conclusion, 'The lever is request size, not code placement' (current-state.md:2021-2030) — that paragraph derives a 19x from batching, then never reaches the swap path, because page-cluster had already been rejected on VMA-mode evidence. Risk is bounded in-kernel: `swapin_nr_pages()` (mm/swap_state.c:658-676) shrinks the window back toward 1 when `swapin_readahead_hits` falls, so a workload with no locality self-corrects.

mm/swap_state.c:697-745 — swap_cluster_readahead() reads an aligned physical block under one blk_plug; mm/swap_state.c:658-676 — swapin_nr_pages() adapts the window down on misses

title: vm.swappiness=10 rests on a premise XIP destroyed: nothing cheap is on the file LRU any more
layer: kernel mm tuning (sysctl), no code change
mechanism: 99-s31-memory.conf sets swappiness=10 with an explicit justification: 'Moving the libraries and the fonts into XIP flash inverted [the trade]. A file page evicted now costs a cheap re-read from memory-mapped flash; an anonymous page evicted costs an SD swap round-trip. So the kernel should throw away file pages and keep the heap.' That premise is now false in the strict sense, because cramfs XIP pages are NOT page-cache pages at all: `cramfs_physmem_mmap()` uses `remap_pfn_range()` / VM_MIXEDMAP on flash PFNs (fs/cramfs/inode.c:355-420), which is why libpixman reports Rss 16 kB against 388 kB. Pages that are never allocated are never on the LRU and can never be chosen for reclaim. So the file LRU on this board contains ONLY SD-backed pages — the game binary's text, prboom's mmap'd WAD, Quake's pak reads, ext4 metadata — every one of which costs a ~2.2 ms transaction to re-read, i.e. the same price as an anonymous page, not a 'cheap re-read'. swappiness=10 therefore instructs the kernel to preferentially evict the expensive-and-hot half (get_scan_count weights file ~190/200 at that value) while protecting anon. The measured symptom is in the tree: prboom 'mmaps the WAD and holds only ~56 KB of 4 MB resident, so every new texture, sprite or sound is an SD read' (S02s31-blockdev). The proposal is to re-derive swappiness against today's LRU composition — arms at 10 / 40 / 60 / 100, fresh boot per arm, on both Doom (file-LRU-dominated) and Quake (anon-dominated) — rather than carry a number whose written reasoning no longer describes the machine. The theoretical optimum is below 100 because evicting anon costs a WRITE that evicting clean file does not, but it is nowhere near 10.
evidence: fs/cramfs/inode.c:355-420 — cramfs_physmem_mmap() calls remap_pfn_range() and vm_flags_set(vma, VM_MIXEDMAP) on flash PFNs; no page-cache folio, no LRU entry

title: Buy the fullscreen client real headroom by pre-evicting the idle platform set with process_madvise(MADV_PAGEOUT) before launch
layer: platform userspace (lvdesk's launcher / a small helper), stock kernel syscall
mechanism: Quake runs with MemAvailable at 316 kB against min_free_kbytes=1024. In that state essentially every folio the kernel must allocate — including the folio for each of the 1282 swap-ins — is allocated below the low watermark, so the allocator enters direct reclaim in the faulting task's own context, and direct reclaim of an anonymous page requires a synchronous ~2.5 ms swap WRITE before the allocation can succeed. That cost is charged to nobody: it is not a major fault, and it is invisible because CONFIG_VM_EVENT_COUNTERS is off so pgscan_direct/pgsteal_direct do not exist. The fix does not need a kernel change or a new policy: `process_madvise(pidfd, iov, MADV_PAGEOUT)` is remote-valid in 7.1 (mm/madvise.c:1561-1572) and lets a platform helper push the cold anonymous pages of bluetoothd, dbus-daemon, udevd, wpa_supplicant, crond and lvdesk's own idle allocations out in ONE plugged batch, on CPU1, before the game is exec'd — converting many scattered 2.5 ms synchronous writes inside the game's frame loop into one background burst of merged sequential writes. It has a second-order benefit that compounds with the physical-cluster readahead proposal: pages evicted in one deliberate pass land in contiguous, homogeneous swap slots, which is precisely what makes swap_cluster_readahead's hit rate high on the way back in. lvdesk already spawns the client, so this is our code calling a stock syscall on an unmodified app's neighbours — the app itself is never touched.
evidence: mm/madvise.c:1561-1572 — process_madvise_remote_valid() permits MADV_COLD, MADV_PAGEOUT, MADV_WILLNEED, MADV_COLLAPSE on a remote mm; CONFIG_ADVISE_SYSCALLS=y in the built config

title: The paging lens is being measured blind: CONFIG_VM_EVENT_COUNTERS is off, so swap readahead hits, direct reclaim and pswpin/out do not exist
layer: kernel Kconfig, diagnostic build only (alongside DIAG= and PROF=)
mechanism: Every paging decision on this board is currently judged by two numbers: fps, which carries a documented +-10% per-boot lottery that swamps anything under 10%, and majflt from /proc/<pid>/stat, which counts faults but says nothing about their cost or their cause. The counters that would settle these questions are compiled out: `CONFIG_VM_EVENT_COUNTERS is not set` in the built .config removes `swap_ra` and `swap_ra_hit` (the direct hit-rate readout for the physical-cluster proposal), `pswpin`/`pswpout` (swapbench already warns that its '0 pages swapped in' line is this counter lying, not the swap), and `pgscan_direct`/`pgsteal_direct`/`pgscan_kswapd` (the only way to see whether the game is direct-reclaiming). The symbol is `default y` in mm/Kconfig and costs one per-CPU array of ~NR_VM_EVENT_ITEMS unsigned longs — under 1 kB on a 2-CPU board — with no debugfs, no sysfs tree and no slab growth, so unlike CONFIG_DEBUG_FS (1.14 MB) it can plausibly ship. CONFIG_PSI is a heavier second step (per-task scheduler accounting) but gives /proc/pressure/memory and /proc/pressure/io, which measure the one quantity this whole lens is about — wall-clock lost to memory and I/O stalls — directly, per-cgroup-less, and without an fps lottery; it should be a diagnostic-only arm with CONFIG_PSI_DEFAULT_DISABLED so `psi=1` turns it on for a run. Build them the way PROF=1 is already built: a flag in the Makefile, not a shipping default.
evidence: built kernel .config (via ./docker/build.sh on /src/build/linux/.config) — '# CONFIG_VM_EVENT_COUNTERS is not set', '# CONFIG_PSI is not set', '# CONFIG_CGROUPS is not set'

docs/smp-finish-plan.md:158-162 — 'The Quake per-boot lottery is +-10%... This swing is larger than every lever tried, so two Quake boots cannot judge anything under ~10%'
mm/swap_state.c:445-448 and 735-737 — swapin_readahead_hits / count_vm_event(SWAP_RA): the readahead hit rate is recorded in exactly the counters that are compiled out
docs/current-state.md (DIAG=0 measurement) — CONFIG_DEBUG_FS costs 1.14 MB and was rightly removed; VM_EVENT_COUNTERS is three orders of magnitude cheaper and is being treated the same way
magnitude_estimate: No fps by itself. It is the difference between a proposal that can be accepted or rejected in 3 boots on a counter with a clean signal (swap_ra_hit / swap_ra, pgsteal_direct) and one that needs 8+ boots to beat a +-10% lottery on fps and still cannot say why it moved. Given that the three paging proposals above are each worth single-digit percent — i.e. entirely inside the lottery — this is the gate on all of them. Cost: <1 kB of RAM for VM_EVENT_COUNTERS; PSI stays diagnostic-only.
rule_check: Build-option only, in the pattern the tree already uses for DIAG and PROF. No application touched. Apps stay on SD. Nothing disabled — this ADDS counters. No upstream code patched (these are stock Kconfig symbols). Not a slab lever: VM_EVENT_COUNTERS is a static per-CPU array, not slab, and does not register a single kernfs node.
prior_attempts: Dead-end register #42 ('Kernel static RAM and debug trims') records what was correctly removed — FTRACE -1,056,072 B, DEBUG_FS 1.14 MB, LOG_BUF 264 KiB — and register #41 ('Measurement traps') records twelve ways instruments have lied here, including 'profile=2 allocates ~4 MB' and '/proc/stat over-counts 2.7x'. title: Unbind the framebuffer console at the start of rcS: each scrolled console line is a 768 kB PSRAM memmove, and ~300 init lines scroll it
layer: init script (buildroot-external overlay), one line
mechanism: Writing to /dev/tty0 costs ~8 ms per scrolled line on this board — measured as 0.95 s for 100 lines to tty0 against 0.15 s to /dev/null and 0.27 s to the 1 Mbps serial console. That 8 ms is one full-screen 800x480x16 = 768,000-byte move in PSRAM at roughly 96 MB/s, which is fbcon in SCROLL_MOVE with no acceleration to use. Boot prints ~185 kernel lines plus ~300 init lines to both consoles, so roughly 2-3 s of boot-to-desktop is spent memmoving the framebuffer. The mechanism to stop it already exists and is already trusted: lvdesk unbinds vtcon1 on the way in (so that tearing down fbdev cannot race a console writer — the LCD driver's handover comment says exactly this), and S40lvdesk rebinds it on stop. Moving that unbind to the top of rcS costs nothing new and loses nothing: the kernel boot log — the part that is actually read off the panel — stays on screen frozen, the serial console keeps every byte at full loglevel, and hart0's splash is unaffected. It also makes the DRM console-client handover strictly safer, since there is no writer for even longer. Unlike `loglevel=4`, which the tree explicitly declined to decide ('a taste decision, recorded here rather than made'), this keeps every message on the wire and only stops repainting the panel with them.

Boot prints 185 kernel lines... plus ~300 init lines to both consoles: roughly 2-3 s.'

title: Re-run the SD read_ahead_kb sweep on a verified-quiet board: 128 kB ships only because the evidence for 64 kB was voided, not because it lost
layer: init script sysfs setting (S02s31-blockdev)
mechanism: Readahead on this board is a two-sided trade that the per-transaction floor makes unusually sharp: a bigger window costs almost nothing in wire time (2.49 ms + size/48 MB/s) but every byte it drags in evicts a byte of a 15.4 MB machine whose MemAvailable under a fullscreen game is 316 kB. The one clean sweep against a real client measured 64 kB beating 128 kB on BOTH axes — 101 major faults for 5.0 MB read against 120 faults for 9.4 MB — and 32 kB beating it too (141 faults / 4.4 MB). That sweep was then withdrawn in full, not because it was contradicted but because stray benchmark drivers had survived a `pkill -f` (which busybox does not implement) and were starting and killing games throughout the window. The script reverted to 128 kB and records the instruction it never carried out: 'Re-run the sweep on a board verified quiet first.' This is the cheapest outstanding item in the lens, the direction is documented, and it interacts with the swappiness proposal (a smaller file readahead window makes a higher swappiness less destructive) and with the physical-cluster proposal (they pull in opposite directions on request size, for the right reason: swap slots have physical locality, a random WAD lump does not).

On Doom's measured hitching (41 faults / 1.5 MB inside 1.7 s) that is a few percent of wall time and a visibly shorter tail; on Quake it mostly shows up as less page-cache pressure against the heap. title: Turn off the HRTICK / HRTICK_DL scheduler features - 7.1 silently switched them ON, and each arm is an M-mode ecall
layer: kernel scheduler + RISC-V clockevent (runtime toggle via /sys/kernel/debug/sched/features; one-line patch to ship)
mechanism: In 7.1 `kernel/sched/features.h` guards the HRTICK defaults with `#ifdef CONFIG_HRTIMER_REARM_DEFERRED`, and that symbol is `def_bool y` whenever GENERIC_ENTRY && HAVE_GENERIC_TIF_BITS && HIGH_RES_TIMERS && SCHED_HRTICK. riscv selects HAVE_GENERIC_TIF_BITS, the Makefile enables HIGH_RES_TIMERS, and SCHED_HRTICK is `def_bool HIGH_RES_TIMERS` - so this kernel runs with HRTICK=true and HRTICK_DL=true, where every Linux before 7.x defaulted them off. HRTICK arms a per-rq hardware timer at the current task's virtual deadline on every fair enqueue (`hrtick_update` from `enqueue_task_fair`) and every pick (`set_next_task_fair`), whenever more than one task is runnable. On this board each consequence is unusually dear: (a) the rearm is a clockevent program, and with no Sstc in the hart's ISA the riscv clockevent takes the `sbi_set_timer` branch - an ecall into M-mode OpenSBI, which then does a CSR write plus four CLIC byte writes plus three MTIMECMP word writes; (b) the slice-end expiry is an extra timer interrupt (it plausibly accounts for the gap between the ~100/s tick + ~42/s vblank hrtimer and the ~227/s actually observed on CPU0 under Quake); (c) the expiry forces a preemption that a PREEMPT_NONE kernel would otherwise have taken at the next 10 ms tick, and a context switch here costs ~157 us plus an I-cache refill from 80 MHz flash; (d) under SMP, `hrtick_start` on a remote rq goes through `smp_call_function_single_async`, i.e. an extra IPI into the FreeRTOS-hosted CPU1 on top of the wakeup IPI. HRTICK exists to make slice accounting exact on machines where reprogramming a timer is a local register write; here it is a machine-mode trap, and the workload is three tasks, not a thousand. Because XIP_KERNEL blocks HAVE_ARCH_JUMP_LABEL, `sched_feat()` compiles to a runtime read of `sysctl_sched_features`, and `debugfs_create_file("features", 0644, ...)` is registered unconditionally in 7.1 - so on any DIAG=1 build this is a pure runtime A/B: `echo NO_HRTICK > /sys/kernel/debug/sched/features`, flip back, no reflash.

title: Give the fullscreen (mode-scaled) framebuffer its own PRESENT ioctl - stop paying a full DRM atomic commit on every game frame
layer: kernel DRM driver (esp32s31-lcd) + lvdesk/kms.c
mechanism: The direct-scanout path already avoids the atomic commit: `kms_dirty_rects()` issues DRM_IOCTL_ESP32S31_PRESENT, which is just a cache writeback of the damaged rows. The fullscreen path does not. `kms_fs_dirty()` calls DRM_IOCTL_MODE_DIRTYFB unconditionally, and it must, because `esp32s31_lcd_present_ioctl()` requires the plane's current fb to be `lcd->scan_gem` and returns -EINVAL for the client-sized mode buffer. So every frame of every fullscreen game builds a drm_atomic_state, duplicates plane state, allocates a damage-clips property blob (kvzalloc + idr), takes the ww modeset locks, runs `drm_atomic_helper_commit` and `wait_for_dependencies`, and frees it all - to deliver four integers to a driver whose real work is one `esp32s31_ppa_scale_rect_async` call. That overhead is size-independent: a single 64x16 commit (2 kB of damage) was measured at 1.62 ms, and the code comment in kms.c records 2.2 ms per 320x200 frame against 'the cache writeback of each rectangle' for PRESENT. Everything the new path needs is already factored out and reachable outside the commit: `esp32s31_lcd_copy_one`, the CPU/PPA engine dispatcher, `esp32s31_ppa_scale_rect_async` and `esp32s31_lcd_flush_range`. The safety guard is the one the existing ioctl already uses - take `lcd->pipe.plane.mutex`, verify the plane's fb is the mode fb we were handed, otherwise fall back to DIRTYFB. This is the same shape as the win that replaced the X server: remove a layer whose contract the workload does not need.

title: Scope the touchscreen idle-poll backoff so the measured +3.8% can actually be taken
layer: kernel input driver (gt1158_polled module params, already 0644) + lvdesk policy
mechanism: The GT1158 has no wired INT line, so it is polled: 20 ms while touched, backing off to 60 ms after 25 quiet polls. Each poll is not one event but a chain - a delayed-work timer fires, a kworker is woken, an I2C read of the status register sleeps on its completion (one IRQ), then an I2C write to ack the register (another IRQ), then back. Under a fullscreen Quake timedemo that shows up as 44 i2c IRQ/s on CPU0, i.e. ~17 complete wake-work-sleep-wake cycles a second spent asking a panel nobody is touching whether anyone is touching it. On a board where a wake plus switch is ~157 us and every device IRQ lands on CPU0, this is a textbook event that costs far more than the work it carries. Deepening the backoff to the driver's own 500 ms ceiling was already measured at +3.8% on cpubench and then withdrawn - not because it failed, but because first-touch latency would become half a second. That objection is scope, not physics: the deep backoff is only unacceptable while touch is a plausible input. lvdesk knows when it is not - `fs_active` is set when a client owns the panel, and it already tracks which pointer devices exist. Have lvdesk write `idle_poll_ms` (500 while a fullscreen client owns the panel or a USB mouse is present, 60 otherwise) through the existing 0644 module parameter, which the driver re-reads on every poll by design. The measured gain is taken exactly where it cannot be felt.

title: Stop the LCD's per-frame interrupt that does nothing - 52 IRQ/s on CPU0 carrying zero work
layer: kernel DRM driver (esp32s31-lcd interrupt mask)
mechanism: `esp32s31_lcd_pipe_enable()` unmasks LCD_INT_MASK = VSYNC | TRANS_DONE | UNDERRUN unconditionally. But the handler only *acts* on VSYNC/TRANS_DONE when the `hw_vblank` module parameter is set, and `hw_vblank` defaults to false and is documented as a knob you turn on only after confirming the counters tick. With the default, every one of those interrupts does two MMIO reads, one MMIO write and four counter increments, then returns - a full CLIC entry and generic-entry exit per panel frame for diagnostics. That is 52 IRQ/s on CPU0 during a game, the largest single device-interrupt source in the placement measurement, and it is the cleanest available answer to 'where could the event count itself be cut'. The fix is to unmask only LCD_UNDERRUN_INT (which is a genuine fault signal worth keeping) unless `hw_vblank` is set, and to rewrite the enable register from a `module_param_cb` setter so hw_vblank stays a live runtime knob - the property the existing comment says must be preserved. The same argument applies with less force to the emulated-vblank hrtimer (42/s, `drm_crtc_handle_vblank` with no vblank users, because lvdesk uses SETCRTC + DIRTYFB/PRESENT and never page-flips), but that one carries a recorded trap: keying it on `.enable_vblank` refcounting once left armed flip events undelivered and stopped Weston repainting, so it should only be touched by arming it from `pipe_update` when an event is actually armed, and is the smaller half of the win.
