title: Derive lvdesk's frame gate from the panel's real 42.1 Hz period instead of the hardcoded 16 ms '60 Hz panel'
layer: lvdesk main loop
mechanism: lvdesk paces its LVGL pass with `#define FRAME_MS 16 /* 60 Hz panel */`, but this panel refreshes at 42.1 Hz - a 23.75 ms period, which the driver computes exactly and exports as `frame_period_ns` in debugfs, and which lvdesk itself already has in the mode it set with SETCRTC. So the loop declares a frame due 62.5 times a second against a display that can show 42, and one pass in three does `cursor_vis_update()` (which walks the window list) plus a full `lv_timer_handler()` whose output the panel can never display. It is also internally inconsistent: LVGL's own refresh period is 24 ms, so most of the extra passes find LVGL's refresh timer not due and are pure loop overhead - a poll round trip, two `clock_gettime` syscalls (musl riscv32 has no vDSO time path, so both are real syscalls at 2.8-7.2 us), and the input/ctl drain. The change is to read the CRTC's mode and compute FRAME_MS from it at kms_open() time, keeping an env override for A/B, so the gate follows the panel if the mode ever changes.

title: Program the clockevent from S-mode instead of by SBI ecall - this hart has no Sstc, so every timer arm is a machine-mode trap
layer: kernel clocksource/clockevent driver (a small esp32s31 clockevent) + OpenSBI platform/PMP
mechanism: `riscv_clock_next_event()` uses `csr_write(CSR_STIMECMP, ...)` only when `riscv_sstc_available`; this hart's DT lists no `sstc` extension, so every single clockevent program falls through to `sbi_set_timer()` - an ecall that traps to machine mode, where OpenSBI's `esp32s31_timer_event_start()` writes MINTTHRESH, four CLIC control bytes for ID 7 and three MTIMECMP words before returning. That happens on every hrtimer interrupt, every hrtimer_start that becomes the new earliest, and (as OpenSBI's own commit message records) on every exit from idle. The registers involved are plain MMIO in the 0x10000000 window, the CLIC has a proven-sound S-mode alias at +0x10000, and OpenSBI already configures ID 7 for direct S-mode delivery - so a driver-provided clockevent could arm the timer with three writes from supervisor mode and never leave S-mode. This is the mechanism that makes proposal 1 expensive here, and it is worth doing second: with HRTICK off the rearm count drops sharply, so measure proposal 1 first and only chase this if the residual rate justifies it.

title: The CPU has four per-region cache-policy bits (PMA no-write-allocate / write-through / no-read-allocate) and every one of them is at its default — the 768 kB framebuffer stream owns the shared 64 kB D-cache for free
layer: hart1 PMA CSRs programmed in bootloader/main/core1_trampoline.S, plus the DRM LCD driver's flush path
mechanism:
ESP32-S31's RISC-V core implements Physical Memory Attributes as 16 CSR pairs (CSR_PMACFG0 0xBC0 / CSR_PMAADDR0 0xBD0), and the attribute word carries four cache-policy bits above the usual R/W/X/EN/L: PMA_NONCACHEABLE BIT(27), PMA_WRITETHROUGH BIT(26), PMA_WRITEMISSNOALLOC BIT(25), PMA_READMISSNOALLOC BIT(24). Nothing in ESP-IDF, in our loader, in OpenSBI or in the kernel ever sets bits 24-26 on any target. On hart1 (Linux's CPU0) the entire PMA configuration is ONE entry written by our own trampoline: pmaaddr7 = 0x147fffff, pmacfg7 = 0xe000001d — a locked NAPOT window over all 64 MiB of cached PSRAM with EN|R|W|X and no policy bits, i.e. write-back, write-allocate, read-allocate for every byte of memory the machine has. Fifteen PMA entries on hart1 are unprogrammed, PMA is hart-local (so hart0/FreeRTOS/the radios are untouched), TOR mode gives 4-byte granularity, and the trampoline runs on every boot before Linux, so the lock bit is not an obstacle.

The target is the one physical range that is written hardest and reused least: the scanout buffer at the base of the framebuffer CMA pool (0x50800000, fixed and measured constant). lvdesk paints into it directly (direct scanout), so up to 768,000 bytes per frame stream through a 64 KiB D-cache that BOTH harts share — 11.7 complete cache fills per frame, at up to 42 Hz. Every one of those lines is allocated, is never read again, and evicts something that is. Then the LCD driver must write them all back by hand: esp32s31_lcd_flush_range() calls dma_sync_single_for_device(DMA_TO_DEVICE) at fourteen call sites in the commit path, and it was significant enough that someone already wired dbg_flush_ns / dbg_flush_ns_max / dbg_flush_bytes / dbg_flushes into debugfs to count it.

Three arms, cheapest first, each a two-word edit to the trampoline plus a reboot: (a) split entry 7 into TOR pieces and give [scanout .. scanout+768000) PMA_WRITEMISSNOALLOC — the framebuffer stream stops allocating lines at all, leaving the 64 KiB cache to Quake's user code (59% of CPU0) and the kernel (32%); (b) add PMA_WRITETHROUGH to the same range — the data is in PSRAM as it is written, so every esp32s31_lcd_flush_range() becomes a no-op and the driver's own counter measures the deletion directly; (c) PMA_READMISSNOALLOC over the JPEG/PPA source ranges so capture and blit reads do not evict either. This is emphatically NOT the 0xC0000000 bypass alias (dead-ended at 7.6 MB/s): that is non-cacheable AND unbuffered; no-write-allocate keeps the normal buffered write path and only stops line allocation.

The deletable one is exact and already instrumented: every dma_sync_single_for_device in the commit path disappears under WRITETHROUGH, and debugfs dbg_flush_ns/dbg_flushes reports the saving on the first boot with no new tooling. If a meaningful share of their misses are conflict misses caused by the display stream, this is the only lever in the whole review that speeds up the application's own code without touching the application. Round 1's CACHE_L1_DBUS{0,1}_ACS_{MISS,CONFLICT,NXTLVL_RD}_CNT counters price it before any of this is built — run them with the desktop idle and with fullscreen Quake and subtract.

Apps stay on SD; this changes nothing about paging (it is a cache-policy bit on a physically fixed reserved region, not a placement change). No feature disabled — Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and sound are unaffected, and PMA is hart-local so hart0's radios keep their existing attributes exactly. No upstream code patched: the edit is our trampoline plus, at most, a constant in our own LCD driver. Zero RAM cost — it is CSR bits, not memory. Reversible by reverting two words; every arm is a separate boot, so 'fresh boot per arm' is satisfied by construction.

Write-combining was examined at the software level (memory note s31-write-combine-streams: free for one stream, 18x for three) but never as a hardware region attribute. Cache geometry was correctly closed as fixed (dead end #95, CACHE_L1_DCACHE_BLOCKSIZE/CACHESIZE_CONF are HRO) — this proposal changes policy, not geometry, so that closure does not apply. Round 1 proposed the cache access counters, critical-word-first/early-restart, I-cache prelock and the autoload prefetchers; none of them is a per-region allocation policy. Also settled while looking: the flash MMU CANNOT be used to overlay kernel text into PSRAM (SOC_MMU_PER_EXT_MEM_TARGET = 1 and mmu_ll_write_entry forces the target from the mmu_id, so a 0x4xxxxxxx entry can never point at PSRAM), and the CPU cannot exceed 320 MHz (rtc_clk.c aborts on anything but 320/160/80/53; CPLL is 320 and the only other source is PLL_F240M), with MEM_CLK 160 / SYS_CLK 106.67 / APB 53.33 MHz already at their documented ceilings.

title: Posted writes are OFF on this SoC's CPU and SDMMC bridges — the same bit ships ON on the ESP32-P4, and nothing in IDF or our tree ever writes it
layer: HP_SYSTEM ICM H2X bridge configuration (bootloader init or an early kernel write), plus the PSRAM MSPI arbiter
mechanism:
HP_SYSTEM_ICM_H2X_CFG_REG (DR_REG_HP_SYS_BASE + 0x138) has HP_SYSTEM_CPU_ICM_H2X_POST_WR_EN at bit 0, R/W, **default 0**, and HP_SYSTEM_SDMMC_ICM_H2X_POST_WR_EN at bit 3, R/W, **default 0**. With posting off, a store that crosses the AHB-to-AXI bridge is not acknowledged until it has completed at the far side: the CPU stalls for a full bridge round trip on every MMIO register write and on every uncached store, and the SDMMC's DMA master waits for each write burst into PSRAM to retire rather than streaming.

The decisive evidence that this is a reset-default accident and not a design intent is the sibling part: in /opt/esp-idf/components/soc/esp32p4/register/hw_ver1/soc/hp_system_reg.h:1032 and hw_ver3, the identical field `cpu_icm_h2x_post_wr_en` has **default: 1**. Same IP block, opposite reset value, and a grep of every .c in ESP-IDF finds no code that writes the field on any target — so on the P4 posting is on because the hardware says so and nobody thinks about it, and on the S31 it is off for the same reason. This is precisely the s31-vendor-hal-reset-defaults shape: a field with no setter means the block runs on its reset default.

What pays for it here: APB is CPLL/6 = 53.33 MHz and SYS_CLK is CPLL/3 = 106.67 MHz against a 320 MHz core, so a non-posted peripheral write is tens of core cycles minimum. Every device interrupt on CPU0 pays three CLIC MMIO writes; the SD host driver, the LCD controller, the CLIC, the GPIO/I2C paths and the doorbell all write registers in their hot paths; and on the lent hart every guest trap stores thirteen words into LP-domain memory (see the world-switch proposal), all of which are non-posted today. A companion knob in the same family, also never written by IDF: the PSRAM MSPI has a two-requester arbiter whose settings are all zero — SPI_MEM_S_ARB_WEI_EN default 0, SPI_MEM_S_ARB_REQ0_PRI (AXI read) default 0, SPI_MEM_S_ARB_REQ1_PRI (AXI write) default 0, weights 0 — so a demand cache refill that stalls the pipeline is arbitrated equally against a buffered writeback or a DMA write that stalls nothing. Setting read priority above write is one bit.

Both are single register writes, testable as separate boot arms, and revertible by writing zero.

/Users/gadyke/esp32-s31-linux/bootloader/main/s31_vcpu_world.S:83-89 — the lent CPU's world switch stores to LP-domain memory on every trap, all non-posted today
magnitude_estimate: Small-to-medium and broad rather than deep: it does not remove work, it removes a stall on every MMIO write the machine makes. Sizeable if the bridge round trip is long (plausibly 30-100 core cycles at 53.33 MHz APB): the 6.4% of CPU0 in IRQ/CLIC/entry, the SD host's per-request register traffic against a 2.49 ms request cost, and the lent hart's per-trap store burst are the three places it would show. Honest band 1-4% on Quake, with the SD and cross-hart paths as the likeliest places to see it first. The cheapest decisive test is not a game at all: time a tight loop of writel() to a scratch peripheral register with the bit off and on, then re-run pingpong same-hart and cross-hart. The MSPI read-priority companion is smaller again and should be measured as its own arm, not folded in.
rule_check: No application involvement of any kind. No feature disabled. No upstream code patched — the write goes in our bootloader's init or an early kernel platform hook, both ours. Zero RAM cost. Apps and paging are untouched. The one real hazard is ordering, and it is named and bounded: with posting on, a write that acknowledges an interrupt can retire after the handler returns and re-fire it, so the CLIC and any driver whose IRQ-ack relies on write completion needs a read-back; the drivers in question (CLIC, LCD, PPA, SD) are ours to audit, and the whole thing reverts with one register write, which also makes it a clean runtime toggle in the sense CLAUDE.md prefers.
prior_attempts: Never proposed or tried in any form — the ICM H2X bridge appears nowhere in the repo, the docs, the dead-end register or round 1. Round 1's 'AXI interconnect QoS serve the cache refill' is a different block (ICM master QoS priorities via axi_icm_ll) and a different mechanism (arbitration between masters, not write posting at the bridge); the MSPI arbiter companion is different again (read-vs-write arbitration inside the PSRAM memory controller, one level below the interconnect). Related dead ends that do not cover this: 'Flash mode/clock as a lever' (harvested, QIO-80 is the S31 maximum) and 'cpufreq is inert'. Note also settled during this sweep: PSRAM is already Octal at 250 MHz with ECC off (bootloader/sdkconfig:2721-2731), so the memory device itself is not the constraint — GDMA's measured 210 MB/s copy is already near the device limit while the CPU manages 102, which is what points at the CPU-side write path.

title: The 2D-DMA has memory-to-memory channels with true 2D block descriptors, and the one reason the GDMA damage copy was rejected — 384 descriptors per rectangle — does not exist on it
layer: drivers/gpu/drm/espressif (the PPA driver already owns the 2D-DMA registers) and the LCD commit path
mechanism:
The GDMA damage-copy experiment was rejected on a cost that is specific to a 1-D engine: 'DIRTYFB 10.6 ms vs 7.9 (CPU); 640x384 needs 384 descriptors at ~479 us each'. AXI GDMA is linear, so a strided rectangle costs one descriptor per row and the per-descriptor overhead swamps the transfer. The 2D-DMA is a different engine with a different descriptor format: it has a block descriptor port (DMA2D_OUT_DSCR_PORT_BLK with separate H and V block dimensions, DMA2D_OUT_DSCR_PORT_EN, per-channel burst length, macro-block size and reorder) so one descriptor pair describes a whole rectangle with stride. It also exposes memory-to-memory operation directly: SOC_DMA2D_TRIG_PERIPH_M2M_TX and _M2M_RX exist as first-class peripheral selections ('any value of 4~7 TX, 3~7 RX'), and the instance has 4 TX and 3 RX channels while PPA SRM/blend use peri_sel 1/2/3 and the JPEG codec uses 0 — there is spare capacity.

Feasibility here is unusually good because none of it is new ground: our own esp32s31-ppa.c already programs the 2D-DMA directly (it maps the dma2d register window, its clkrst and its mem-lp control from the DTS, and drives OUT_CONF0, OUT_LINK_CONF, OUT_DSCR_PORT_BLK and the RX side by hand), and the completion signal is already understood and shipped — operations complete on the 2D-DMA receive EOF, not the PPA's own EOF, which is the fix that took a 64x64 blend from 1,322 us to 169 us. An M2M pair is an increment on working code in the same driver, not a new engine bring-up.

What it buys: the fullscreen damage copy moves off the CPU at engine bandwidth (GDMA measured 210 MB/s, PPA 153, CPU 102) as ONE descriptor rather than 384, and — the part that matters more than the raw rate — it becomes asynchronous work that can overlap the next frame under late present, instead of 7.9 ms of CPU0 that lvdesk must spend before it can do anything else.

magnitude_estimate: Small-to-medium, and bounded by what the display path costs at all: lvdesk is ~30% of a core and DIRTYFB is 1.62-7.9 ms per commit depending on damage. A 768 kB rectangle at 210 MB/s is ~3.7 ms of engine time against 7.9 ms of CPU, so a synchronous swap is worth roughly half the copy; the asynchronous form is worth the whole of it if it can be overlapped with late present, which is already shipped and already worth +13% on Doom. Realistic band 2-5% on Quake, better on Doom. Two things could kill it and both are cheap to check first: the dead-end rule that offload cannot win below ~128 kB (a full-screen rectangle is 6x that, so the rule does not bite, but partial damage will), and the observation that gdma_copy pre-empted other engines (DIRTYFB -27% with it off) — so this must be measured with the JPEG recorder idle and with it running.
rule_check: Application untouched — this is entirely inside our DRM driver. No upstream code patched: the 2D-DMA has no mainline driver and the PPA driver is ours. Apps stay on SD and paging is unaffected. No feature disabled. RAM cost is a descriptor pair (tens of bytes), not buffers — the 915 kB of persistent JPEG buffers that were reverted are not being reintroduced. Must be built behind a runtime toggle in the existing debugfs/module-param style, like ppa_min_bytes and gdma_copy, so the arms are a knob rather than a rebuild.

The 2D-DMA itself was examined once and correctly dismissed for a different question: 'DMA2D has no CLUT either ... it is not an alternative expander' (current-state.md:6874) — that rules it out as a palette engine, not as a copy engine, and nothing in the repo, the docs or round 1 has ever proposed it as one. 'Offload isn't purchasable' (memory note) is the governing prior and is respected by restricting this to large rectangles. title: Every trap on the lent CPU pays thirteen diagnostic stores into LP-domain memory — on a path where the doorbell itself was measured at 0.66 us of 165
layer: bootloader/main/s31_vcpu_world.S (hart0 vCPU world switch)
mechanism:
The cross-hart crossing costs ~165 us and the two components anyone has measured are tiny: the doorbell ISR to the vCPU task running again is 0.66 us over 9,072 samples, and the FPU world swap is ~0.2 us. ~164 us is unaccounted for, and the structure of the code says where to look. s31_vcpu_world_out and s31_vcpu_world_in run on EVERY guest-to-M-mode trap — the exception path, the interrupt path and the timer path all call world_out (s31_vcpu_asm.S:119, 171, 221) and s31_vcpu_resume calls world_in (:248) — so their cost is not per-crossing, it is per-trap, and the lent CPU takes a trap for every emulated interrupt, every SBI ecall and every emulated CSR access that Linux's wake path makes.

Inside them is an unconditional diagnostic tax. The `mark` macro does two stores: one to 0x50FEFFD0 (PSRAM mailbox) and one to s31_vcpu_trace. world_out executes marks 0x11, 0x12, 0x13, 0x16, 0x0f plus four direct stores into s31_vcpu_trace[3..6]; world_in executes 0x21, 0x23, 0x26, 0x0f plus a store to 0x50FEFFF8 labelled 'DIAGNOSTIC: did the enables take?'. That is nine marks plus five extra stores per guest trap round trip: **thirteen stores into s31_vcpu_trace and ten into the PSRAM mailbox, every time**.

s31_vcpu_trace is declared RTC_NOINIT_ATTR (s31_vcpu.c:53) — it lives in the LP TCM at 0x2E000000-0x2E008000, a separate low-power domain reached across the peripheral bus, not in the HP SRAM the rest of the world switch uses. Stores there are the slowest kind this core makes, and they are all non-posted today (see the H2X proposal: CPU_ICM_H2X_POST_WR_EN defaults to 0), so each one is a full bridge round trip and they do not pipeline. Thirteen of those per trap, multiplied by however many traps Linux's wake path takes on the lent hart, is the shape of a missing hundred microseconds.

The fix is deletion, not redesign: keep the two crumb counters that are in HP SRAM and cost nothing, put the marks and the trace stores behind a build flag that is off by default, and keep exactly the ones the post-mortem path genuinely needs (the mcause and guest-PC record in the exception path, which is not the hot path). This is the same failure the project has already recorded three times — 'Diagnostics left on control-flow paths' — and the same one as dev_info() in the per-frame path, which was 15% of the CPU down to 5.5% when removed.

If an LP-domain store is 100-200 core cycles (0.3-0.6 us), thirteen of them is 4-8 us per trap, and Linux's wake path on the lent hart takes many traps — that arithmetic reaches the missing time, but the per-store cost is the number I cannot measure from here and it is the whole claim. It settles in one build: pingpong cross/same ratio over three fresh boots with the marks compiled out, plus the existing s31_xing monitor bracketing world_out/world_in the same way it already bracketed the doorbell. If the ratio does not move, the 165 us is elsewhere and that is worth knowing too, because it eliminates the last cheap suspect and leaves only the emulated-interrupt architecture. If it does move, CPU1 — currently 64% idle while CPU0 runs Quake at 86% — becomes usable for the first time, and every placement result on record (pinned lvdesk +15.3%, co/split 16.43 vs 13.83) was measured under this tax.

No feature disabled — the radios, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and audio on hart0 are not affected by removing stores from the guest trap path. No upstream code involved. The post-mortem capability is preserved deliberately: the exception path's mcause/PC record stays (it is what produced the irq/chip.o illegal-instruction diagnosis in one build instead of seven), only the unconditional per-trap breadcrumbs go behind a flag. prior_attempts: The crossing has been attacked four times and every attempt targeted something else: the raw-vector doorbell (retracted, worth under 1% — the ISR is 0.66 us of 165), vCPU task priority 1->10 (no change), conditional/lazy FPU save (162 vs 155 us, and the save is <100 cycles), rcu_nocbs (~524 vs 542 us, does not compound with softirq.o). Polling idle on the lent CPU via trapped wfi was tried and was worse (+11% canaries, 460k M-mode traps/s). Hardware S-mode interrupts on hart0 and routing IPIs through M-mode are both impossible. Nobody has looked at what the world switch itself stores, and the two prior FPU measurements would not have caught it because they timed the register swap, not the surrounding breadcrumbs. This proposal also compounds with the H2X posted-write proposal, which would make each of these stores cheaper even if they stay.

title: The shipping kernel is built WITH frame pointers, by accident: PROFILING selected PERF_EVENTS, which selects FRAME_POINTER on riscv, and clearing the selectors never cleared it
layer: kernel build / whole-kernel codegen
mechanism: arch/riscv/Kconfig:102 has `select FRAME_POINTER if PERF_EVENTS || (FUNCTION_TRACER && !DYNAMIC_FTRACE)`. The board's Makefile turns PROFILING on in the base kconfig-tweak list (Makefile:563 `--enable PROFILING`) and only later turns it back off for PROF=0 (Makefile:251 `PROF_TWEAKS := --disable PROFILING --disable PERF_EVENTS`); because the defconfig is not re-applied between builds (Makefile:256-259 says so explicitly), any build that ever had PERF_EVENTS on set FRAME_POINTER=y through the select, and `olddefconfig` then keeps it for ever - `default y if ARCH_WANT_FRAME_POINTERS` makes it user-selectable in its own right. This is the exact failure mode the Makefile itself documents at lines 219-221 for PERF_EVENTS, one level deeper and never noticed. The consequence is that linux-71-port/Makefile:962-963 adds `-fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-optimize-sibling-calls` to every kernel object: each function stores and reloads s0 on the kernel stack and computes a frame pointer, s0 is removed from allocation everywhere, and tail calls are forbidden. On a machine whose kernel text executes XIP from 80 MHz flash at ~6x RAM, and whose kernel-stack traffic lands in the ONE shared D-cache, that is a tax on every kernel call. The fix is a Kconfig choice upstream supports and the board's own defconfig already asks for: add `--disable FRAME_POINTER` to PROF_TWEAKS' PROF=0 arm (and keep it enabled for PROF=1, which needs it).
evidence: linux-71-port/arch/riscv/configs/esp32s31_defconfig:266 - `# CONFIG_FRAME_POINTER is not set` (the intent)

Generated .config (scratchpad config.txt) - `CONFIG_FRAME_POINTER=y` while `# CONFIG_PERF_EVENTS is not set`, `# CONFIG_PROFILING is not set`, `# CONFIG_FTRACE is not set`, `# CONFIG_KALLSYMS is not set`, `# CONFIG_STACKTRACE is not set`: nothing in the shipping kernel consumes the frame chain

linux-71-port/arch/riscv/Kconfig:102 `select FRAME_POINTER if PERF_EVENTS ...`; Makefile:563 `--enable PROFILING`; Makefile:251 PROF_TWEAKS for PROF=0; Makefile:256-259 'the defconfig is not re-applied'

Built vmlinux disassembly (/src/build/linux/vmlinux, 22 Sep): 31,020 of 32,143 functions (96.5%) emit the `addi s0,sp,N` frame-pointer prologue; 86,846 of 1,611,943 instructions (5.39%) and 174,580 of 4,556,156 text bytes (3.83%) are frame-pointer bookkeeping

Weighted by the Quake CPU0 hart0-sampler profile (quake_top.txt, 3,380 kernel samples): frame-pointer instructions are 2.28% of the instruction mix of the sampled functions, 2.84% for the flash-resident ones (2,084 of 3,380 samples are flash text)

The hot path is full of tiny functions where the frame pointer is a large fraction: generic_handle_domain_irq 3 of 11 instructions (27%), do_raw_spin_lock 3/22, handle_irq_desc 3/25, riscv_timer_interrupt 3/22, handle_riscv_irq 3/25, clic_writeb 3/26. generic_handle_domain_irq is a one-line forwarder that cannot tail-call because of -fno-optimize-sibling-calls, so it builds and tears down a whole frame
linux-71-port/arch/riscv/kernel/stacktrace.c:105 has a full `#else /* !CONFIG_FRAME_POINTER */` walk_stackframe, so backtraces degrade to a stack scan rather than disappearing
magnitude_estimate: Small on fps but broad: ~2.3-2.8% of kernel-mode instructions plus two kernel-stack memory accesses per call and the lost sibling-call optimisation. Kernel is 32% of CPU0 during Quake, so roughly 1-2% of CPU0 -> Quake ~16.0 to ~16.2-16.4 fps. The larger prize is 170 KB of linux-partition text: the partition currently has 119,803 B spare, so this more than doubles the slack that has repeatedly forced trades (profiling vs radios; 'whole-kernel -O2 does not fit').
rule_check: PASS. No application is rebuilt, relinked or steered. Apps stay on SD. Nothing functional is disabled - Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and sound are untouched. title: Page-cache-less app reads: set IOCB_DONTCACHE (folio dropbehind) by platform policy, since the app will never call preadv2 itself
layer: kernel mm/VFS policy
mechanism: 7.1 already implements Jens Axboe's uncached buffered I/O end to end - mm/readahead.c:190 sets folio dropbehind from the ractl, mm/filemap.c:1610-1700 has folio_end_dropbehind/filemap_end_dropbehind, include/linux/fs.h has IOCB_DONTCACHE/FOP_DONTCACHE, and fs/ext4/file.c:993 already advertises FOP_DONTCACHE. The only missing piece is that nothing ever sets the flag, because it arrives from userspace as RWF_DONTCACHE on preadv2 and the games use plain read(). The platform can set it without touching the app: a mount option on the SD rootfs, a check in ext4_file_read_iter for sequential read-only regular-file reads past N bytes, or a per-task flag the lvdesk launcher sets on clients it starts. This changes the cost structure rather than tuning a knob: today every 4 KB of pak/wad/level data that a game streams is admitted to the file LRU and has to displace something; with vm.swappiness=10 (overlay/etc/sysctl.d/99-s31-memory.conf) reclaim is aimed almost entirely at the file LRU, so what it displaces is preferentially the app's own mapped text and the data it is about to read again. Dropbehind keeps the streamed bytes out of the LRU at all - the read still happens, the memory never competes. Crucially IOCB_DONTCACHE applies to read()/write() iocbs only, not to page faults, so the app's mmapped text and the XIP library overlay are untouched by construction.
evidence: linux-71-port/mm/filemap.c:1610,1629,1657,1678; linux-71-port/mm/readahead.c:190; linux-71-port/include/linux/fs.h:345,1987,3449; linux-71-port/fs/ext4/file.c:993 - the mechanism is present and ext4 opts in

Quake CPU0 profile shows live read() traffic through ext4 during the timedemo, not just at load: ext4_mpage_readpages 8 samples, __filemap_add_folio 7, filemap_read 3, copy_page_to_iter 3, vfs_read 5, ksys_read 3, __read_end_io 3, ext4_es_lookup_extent 3, workingset_update_node 3 - i.e. new page-cache folios are being admitted while do_swap_page (8), swapin_readahead (2), swap_read_folio (3) show the heap is being paged back in at the same time

overlay/etc/sysctl.d/99-s31-memory.conf: vm.swappiness = 10, vm.page-cluster = 0, vm.min_free_kbytes = 1024, vm.watermark_boost_factor = 0 - reclaim is deliberately aimed at the file LRU, which is exactly the LRU the streamed reads join
Given constants: Quake heap 10 MB with ~6.2 MB in swap, 1,300-1,550 major faults per demo, SD request floor 2.49 ms
magnitude_estimate: Small to medium, and it has a hard ceiling that is worth stating: 1,300-1,550 major faults at the 2.49 ms SD floor is 3.2-3.9 s, and CPU0 is only 9% idle across the demo, so ALL of Quake's paging is worth at most ~9%. A realistic recovery of a third to a half of it is 2-5% (16.0 -> 16.3-16.8 fps). Measure it as major-fault count per demo first (cheap, and it moves or it does not) before measuring fps.
rule_check: PASS. The app is not rebuilt, relinked, wrapped or config-steered - the flag is set by the kernel or by our launcher, which is the same class of platform-side placement as the existing PIE_BOUNCE and lvdesk pinning. Apps stay on SD and still page from SD. No feature is disabled. The upstream mechanism is used as shipped; only the policy that sets the flag is ours, so no mature upstream code is patched.

title: Stop paying a call, a frame and a flash cache line for lock and IRQ helpers that upstream expects to be inlined
layer: kernel build / arch Kconfig
mechanism: Two independent causes leave one-to-three-instruction helpers out of line in flash. First, CONFIG_CC_OPTIMIZE_FOR_SIZE=y makes GCC 15.2 refuse to inline `static inline` helpers that upstream never intended to be real functions: do_raw_spin_lock (include/linux/spinlock.h), mmiowb_spin_lock/mmiowb_spin_unlock/mmiowb_set_pending (asm-generic/mmiowb.h), irq_can_handle and __kstat_incr_irqs_this_cpu (kernel/irq/internals.h) all exist as out-of-line flash symbols in the shipped vmlinux. Second, riscv does not select the ARCH_INLINE_SPIN_* family, so _raw_spin_lock/_raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore and friends stay out of line in spinlock.o even though the board is PREEMPT_NONE, which is the condition kernel/Kconfig.locks requires; s390 selects them and gets them inlined. Both are upstream-supported switches: per-object `-O2`/`-finline-functions` via CFLAGS_<obj>.o or ccflags-y for the objects already in .text..fast, and `select ARCH_INLINE_SPIN_LOCK` etc. in arch/riscv/Kconfig. On this board each avoided out-of-line call is a call, a return, a frame, and a fetch of a separate 80 MHz flash cache line into a 16 KB private I-cache, so it is worth several times what it would be on a normal machine. It is also the natural partner to the frame-pointer proposal: inlining spin_lock everywhere grows text, and dropping frame pointers returns ~170 KB of partition to pay for it.
evidence: Quake CPU0 profile, flash-resident: do_raw_spin_lock 48 samples (22 instructions, 64 B), _raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore 37, _raw_spin_lock 13, _raw_spin_lock_irqsave 8, _raw_spin_lock_irq 3, __raw_spin_unlock 18 across copies, mmiowb_spin_unlock 17, mmiowb_spin_lock 10, mmiowb_set_pending 10, irq_can_handle 14, irq_can_handle_pm 8, __kstat_incr_irqs_this_cpu 9, kstat_incr_irqs_this_cpu 2, cpu_relax 6, trylock 6 - about 209 of 3,380 kernel samples (6.2% of kernel time)

Generated config: CONFIG_CC_OPTIMIZE_FOR_SIZE=y, CONFIG_PREEMPT_NONE=y, CONFIG_DEBUG_SPINLOCK not set and CONFIG_DEBUG_LOCK_ALLOC not set - so do_raw_spin_lock is the non-debug `static inline`, out-of-lined purely by -Os
kernel/Kconfig.locks gates INLINE_SPIN_* on !PREEMPTION && ARCH_INLINE_SPIN_*; arch/riscv/Kconfig selects neither

The dead-end register already establishes the cost model: identical code is 5.98x faster from RAM than from XIP flash, and locking/spinlock.o in .text..fast DOES NOT BOOT - so these symbols cannot be relocated and can only be inlined away
magnitude_estimate: Small. The lock bodies themselves remain; what disappears is the call/return, the frame, and the extra flash line. Recovering a third of the 6.2% of kernel time these wrappers occupy is ~0.6-0.7% of CPU0; a larger -O2 effect on the ~200 KB of RAM-resident .text..fast objects might add another 0.5-1%. Call it 1-2% of CPU0 combined, and it builds and measures in the same arm as the frame-pointer change (rootfs/pingpong same-hart medians, 3 fresh boots, the method that resolved softirq.o at -19.7%). Watch text size: if inlining the spinlocks costs more flash than frame pointers return, drop that half.
rule_check: PASS. No app change; apps stay on SD. No feature disabled. No mature upstream code is patched - per-object CFLAGS and an arch `select` are the upstream-sanctioned ways to do both, and the s390 precedent is in-tree. Costs no RAM; costs flash partition, which the frame-pointer change funds.
prior_attempts: The register has 'Whole-kernel -O2 does not fit (119,803 B slack)' and '-O3 died' (that was the Quake app). Per-object optimisation level has never been tried and is a different lever from placement: the object-granular .text..fast batches (#320 43 kB, rcu/tree.o, SMP objects, DRM commit) all moved code without changing how it was compiled. ARCH_INLINE_SPIN_* appears nowhere in dead-ends.json or the round-1 titles. Note the register's warning that spinlock.o in RAM does not boot - this proposal deliberately does not move it.

title: Hand the global tick duty (tick_do_timer_cpu) to the lent hart, which is already waking 100 times a second anyway
layer: kernel scheduler/timekeeping placement
mechanism: Every previous offload-to-CPU1 idea died on the hand-off: a cross-hart wake is ~165 us and a kworker hand-off ~8 ms (which the board's own Makefile explains at lines 230-234 - PREEMPT_NONE plus HZ=100 makes a jiffy the granularity of every thread hand-off). The global tick duty is the one piece of kernel work that needs no hand-off at all, because CONFIG_HZ_PERIODIC with NO_HZ disabled means CPU1 already takes a tick 100 times a second whether or not it does anything with it. tick_do_timer_cpu is claimed by the boot CPU and never moves; whichever CPU owns it runs tick_do_update_jiffies64, do_timer, update_wall_time/__timekeeping_advance, the NTP work and calc_global_load on top of its own local tick. Setting it to CPU1 once CPU1 is online moves that block off the hot hart. The usual objection - the timekeeper seqlock would ping-pong between caches - does not apply here: there is ONE shared D-cache, so CPU0's ktime_get readers see CPU1's writes without any coherence traffic. That shared-cache property is what makes work migration cheap on this board in a way the general SMP rules do not predict, and this is the cheapest possible test of it.
evidence: Quake CPU0 profile, global tick work: __timekeeping_advance 56 samples (1,606 B, RAM), tick_do_update_jiffies64 21, timekeeping_update_from_shadow 13, calc_global_load 10, update_fast_timekeeper 6, tk_update_leap_state 5, ntp_get_next_leap 4, ntp_tick_length 3, accumulate_nsecs_to_secs 3 = ~121 of 3,380 kernel samples
Generated config: CONFIG_HZ_PERIODIC=y, CONFIG_HZ=100, CONFIG_NO_HZ / NO_HZ_IDLE / NO_HZ_COMMON all off (Makefile:530 TICK_TWEAKS forces this), so CPU1's tick is unconditional and already paid for
Measured constants: CPU1 ~64% idle, ONE shared D-cache, cross-hart wake ~165 us
Makefile:230-234 attributes the ~8 ms hand-off to PREEMPT_NONE + HZ=100, which is why this proposal deliberately uses no hand-off
magnitude_estimate: Small: ~121 of 3,380 kernel samples is ~3.6% of kernel time, ~1.1% of CPU0, so Quake ~16.0 -> ~16.2 fps. Cheap to try (a boot parameter that assigns tick_do_timer_cpu after CPU1 onlines) and cheap to abandon.
rule_check: PASS on the letter of every rule - no app change, apps stay on SD, nothing disabled, no upstream code patched beyond assigning an existing upstream variable (tick_do_timer_cpu is reassigned by upstream itself on hotplug and by NO_HZ_FULL housekeeping). It costs no RAM.
prior_attempts: Not in dead-ends.json or the round-1 titles. Adjacent entries are all hand-off-based and all failed for that reason: 'Deferring the DRM damage copy to a kworker' (2.15-2.26x worse, 107 flush_work waits at 7.4 ms), 'wq+RPS on CPU1' (-7%), 'Moving work to hart0 beyond radios' (SD proxy adds 165 us to a 2.49 ms request), 'Cheapening the cross-hart crossing' (the doorbell ISR is 0.66 us of 165 us). The distinguishing feature here is that no crossing is needed. The relevant warning is the other one: NO_HZ_IDLE 'lost a timer wake: silent hang, ~1 death per 2 runs'.

title: musl's XEspV routines force a cross-hart trap-and-migrate on every libc call that lands on CPU1
layer: musl libc (our XEspV patch) + arch/riscv trap path + scheduler placement
mechanism: The shipped rootfs is built with `-march=...xespv2p2` and our musl patch routes memcpy, memcmp, memchr, memrchr, strcmp and strnlen into PIE vector kernels whenever >=64 bytes remain (docs/xespv-libc.md:1-20). hart0 (CPU1) has no PIE unit, so each of those calls is an illegal instruction there. medeleg is 0xb100 (bit 2 clear), so the trap goes to M-mode OpenSBI first, is redirected to S-mode, and lands in do_trap_insn_illegal -> esp32s31_ext_lent_cpu_illegal, which calls set_cpus_allowed_ptr(current, cpumask_of(boot_cpu)) on the *running* task. That is not a hint: excluding the CPU the task is on goes through stop_one_cpu/migration_cpu_stop, i.e. a forced deschedule, a stopper wake, a migration and a reschedule, followed by a second set_cpus_allowed_ptr to put the old mask back. The I-caches are private, so the task also restarts with a cold 16 KB I-cache on the other hart, and kernel text is XIP flash at ~6x. With PIE_BOUNCE=1000 (Makefile:430) nothing is ever pinned, so a memcpy-heavy task that the load balancer keeps pushing onto the 64%-idle CPU1 can ping-pong indefinitely: balancer moves it to CPU1, the first large memcpy traps, the trap moves it back. TyrQuake is a software rasteriser that calls memcpy constantly. The fix that keeps stock behaviour is to drop the XEspV patch from the shipped musl (returning libc to stock scalar code), so no ordinary process ever traps on the lent hart and the scheduler can use CPU1 freely. Fallbacks if the libc routines must stay: delegate illegal-instruction to S-mode (medeleg bit 2) to remove the M-mode hop, and/or replace the forced migration with something that does not use the stopper.
evidence: linux-71-port/arch/riscv/kernel/esp32s31-ext.c:385-410 - the trap handler calls set_cpus_allowed_ptr(current, cpumask_of(boot_cpu)) and then restores the old mask; no per-task memory of the trap, so the balancer is free to send it back immediately
linux-71-port/arch/riscv/kernel/traps.c:194-210 - every user-mode illegal instruction on the lent CPU reaches that path

title: Swap readahead has only ever been tested in VMA mode, which turns one fault into eight scattered SD requests
layer: kernel mm/swap + runtime sysfs/sysctl
mechanism: swap_use_vma_readahead() is true whenever enable_vma_readahead is set and no swap device is rotational; an SD swapfile is non-rotational, so VMA readahead is what this board uses. swap_vma_readahead() reads pages whose *virtual* addresses neighbour the fault - their swap slots are scattered, so each is its own bio and each pays the flat ~2.0-2.5 ms SD per-request floor. That is why page-cluster 3 measured worse (170 s vs 167 s on Quake; 198.8 vs 201.1 CoreMark on the desktop) and why the sysctl comment concluded 'the extra bytes are fetched and discarded'. swap_cluster_readahead() reads an aligned run of (1 << page_cluster) *swap slots*, which are contiguous in the swapfile, so the plug merges them into ONE request: 2.49 ms + 32/48 MB/s = ~3.2 ms for eight pages against ~20 ms for the same eight as separate faults. Because the SD cost model is flat below 16 KiB, a 4-page cluster is very nearly free. The untried arm is `echo 0 > /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled` plus vm.page-cluster=2 or 3 - two runtime writes, no build.
evidence: linux-71-port/mm/swap_state.c:407-410 - swap_use_vma_readahead() gates on enable_vma_readahead && !nr_rotate_swap; the mmc queue is non-rotational so VMA mode is active
linux-71-port/mm/swap_state.c:681-700 vs 790-810 - cluster readahead reads an aligned block of swap slots ('doesn't cost us any seek time'), VMA readahead reads pages around the fault address
linux-71-port/mm/swap_state.c:908-928 - /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled exists and is writable in this kernel

memory s31-read-is-memory-bound / CLAUDE.md - SD per-request = 2.49 ms + size/48 MB/s with a flat ~2.0 ms floor below 16 KiB, so request SIZE is the only lever

If cluster readahead achieves even a 50% hit rate it collapses ~1,300 requests to ~200-300 and recovers 3-5% of the run; if the hit rate is poor it costs memory pressure on a board with ~1.3 MB MemAvailable and must be reverted. Two runtime writes, one timedemo per arm, fresh boot per arm.

title: The fullscreen present hashes the same 77 KB twice and keeps an index plane nothing else reads
layer: lvdesk/xshim frame path (ShmPutImage handler + fs_present)
mechanism: For a fullscreen indexed client the frame is walked twice. xshim's ShmPutImage handler copies the client's segment into the window's index plane while computing a per-row FNV-1a hash to derive the damage box (xshim.c:5433-5546). lvdesk's fs_present then re-reads those same rows, computes a SECOND per-row FNV-1a hash (lvdesk.c:4727-4755) to decide which rows to skip, and palette-expands into the fullscreen mode buffer. Two independent hash schemes answer the same question - 'did this row change' - over the same bytes, and the index plane between them exists only so that the second pass has somewhere to read from: in fullscreen LVGL's refresh timer is disabled outright (lvdesk.c:4085-4112, fs_render_set), so nothing else ever reads that plane. The structural form is: consume the segment by expanding it straight into the presented plane inside the ShmPutImage handler (which is the legal consumption point - SDL 1.2 XSyncs after every XShmPutImage, so the client is blocked), carry the row-skip decision from the single hash, and let late present defer only the kms_fs_dirty ioctl rather than the whole notify_draw. That removes a full-frame copy (77 KB read + 77 KB write), one whole hash pass, and 77 KB of resident RAM.

lvdesk/lvdesk.c:4727-4755 - fsrh_hash over the same rows again, immediately before the expand
lvdesk/lvdesk.c:4085-4112 - fs_render_set() swaps LVGL's refresh callback for a no-op for the whole fullscreen period, so the index plane has no other consumer
docs/worklog-2026-09-19.md:405-412 - 'ShmPutImage handler 5.7 ms/frame = copy+hash of the 64 KB frame + 3.6 ms expand', i.e. ~2.1 ms of it is the copy at 320x200 (~2.5 ms at Quake's 320x240)

magnitude_estimate: Removes ~2.5 ms/frame of CPU and ~77 KB of RAM at 320x240. Honest caveat on the current SMP build: lvdesk runs mostly on the 64%-idle CPU1, so most of that 2.5 ms is already free, and moving the expand in front of the reply lengthens the client's blocked window by ~0.5 ms. So expect 0-3% fps on SMP, 4-6% on UP and under contention, plus a smaller worst-frame tail. Small, not large - offered because it is a genuine duplicate conversion rather than because it fills a gap.
rule_check: xshim/lvdesk are ours. App untouched; the MIT-SHM contract is honoured more strictly than today (consumption inside the request). No feature disabled, no upstream patched. Frees RAM rather than spending it.
prior_attempts: dead-ends: 'MIT-SHM adoption ... 31.7 fps adopted but flickering ... Illegal' - that attempt adopted the segment and read it LATE, which is exactly what flickers. Row-hash damage, 32-bit FNV and the paired stores are already harvested and are not re-proposed.

title: Fullscreen is the only present path still paying a full atomic commit, and it throws away the row damage it just computed
layer: lvdesk/kms.c + the espressif DRM driver's ioctl surface
mechanism: Two independent cuts in one function. (a) kms_dirty_rects() uses DRM_IOCTL_ESP32S31_PRESENT under direct scanout and only falls back to DIRTYFB; kms_fs_dirty() has no such path and issues DRM_IOCTL_MODE_DIRTYFB unconditionally, so every fullscreen game frame allocates and duplicates atomic state, builds a damage blob, runs drm_atomic_check and the full commit tail. That machinery was measured at 2.2 ms per frame in the windowed path and is exactly what the PRESENT ioctl was added to avoid. The fullscreen case cannot use PRESENT as written (the driver must still PPA-scale the mode buffer into the scanout), so it needs a 'present scaled rect' sibling: the same damage-iteration, lattice snap and esp32s31_lcd_copy_one work the commit already does, reached directly. (b) kms_fs_dirty takes ONE clip, so fs_present collapses its per-row hash result to a bounding box (lvdesk.c:4838-4841, dh = cy1-cy0+1) - when a single status-bar digit changes in Doom, the driver rescales the whole frame. kms_dirty_rects already carries up to KMS_MAX_CLIPS=8 clips for exactly this reason, and the driver iterates a clip list with a copy_rect array. Passing the row runs instead of their bounding box cuts the PPA's scaled area, which is what the next commit blocks on.

lvdesk/lvdesk.c:4961-4975 - fsg_dirty_bucket exists precisely because the dirty call's tail was suspected; the buckets go out to >=12 ms
docs/worklog-2026-09-19.md:407-409 - '+ PRESENT ioctl 33.5, 33.2 / 5420, 5425 (fps-neutral, -3% lvdesk)' is the measured size of cut (a) in the windowed case
magnitude_estimate: (a) ~1.5-2 ms/frame of lvdesk CPU, which the windowed A/B says is fps-neutral and -3% lvdesk; (b) cuts the scaled area on any frame with a static region - for Doom's status bar that is ~16% of the PPA's per-frame work, more for a mostly-still client, and it mainly shows in the dirty tail rather than the mean. Combined: 1-3% fps, a shorter worst frame. Small, and stated as small.
rule_check: Our driver and our compositor; the new ioctl sits alongside the existing private PRESENT ioctl (patches/0049) and touches no upstream DRM code. Apps unchanged, nothing disabled, no RAM cost.
prior_attempts: dead-ends: '.text..fast for the DRM commit path' is dead (under 1% of wall) - this removes the commit rather than speeding it up. 'XLITE-RING, PRESENT ioctl, fast present' harvested cut (a) for the windowed path only. LVDESK_FULLDIRTY exists as the opposite experiment (report MORE damage) and is not this.

title: Chain the PPA's CLUT expand to its scale so no CPU touches a fullscreen game's pixels
layer: lvdesk fullscreen present + esp32s31-ppa/lcd driver
mechanism: Today a fullscreen indexed frame costs the CPU two passes (copy 77 KB, expand 77 KB -> 154 KB) and the PPA one (154 KB -> 768 KB scale). Make the index plane a GEM dumb buffer instead of malloc'd memory, and the copy out of the client's segment lands somewhere the PPA can read by DMA. The present then becomes two chained engine ops with no CPU pixel pass at all: CLUT expand 320x240 indices to RGB565 into the mode buffer, then the scale the driver already runs, both async, one completion. The CPU's remaining work per frame is the 77 KB segment copy and a cache writeback the driver already performs. This is the one form of PPA CLUT that has never been built: every previous arm expanded into cached compositor memory from non-GEM shim pages, which needed a reserved-pool bounce copy and a flush - the cost the register blames for the loss.
evidence: dead-ends.json (PPA CLUT entry) - '320x200: 27.2 vs CPU 29.4/29.9/29.0 fps (-7.5%) ... The SHM segment is not GEM-backed. Fullscreen was rejected without building the chained form'
docs/frame-path-plan.md section 3 - 'the fullscreen arm was not run - the existing code has no chained expand-then-scale path ... That chain remains a possible build, not a measurement'
lvdesk/lvdesk.c:4760-4900 - the CPU expand, measured at 3062 us per 320x240 frame with paired 32-bit stores
linux-71-port/drivers/gpu/drm/espressif/esp32s31-lcd.c:2860-2925 - the driver already picks between async PPA scale entry points per rect, so a second chained op fits the existing dispatcher
memory s31-ppa-completion-signal - completion on 2D-DMA RX EOF took a 64x64 blend from 1,322 to 169 us, which is what makes a second small op affordable at all
CLAUDE.md constants - PPA 153 MB/s vs CPU copy 102 MB/s; the CLUT op is 77 KB in / 154 KB out, ~1.5 ms of engine against ~3.0 ms of CPU
magnitude_estimate: Removes ~3.0 ms/frame of CPU pixel work at 320x240, at the cost of ~1.5 ms more engine time per frame and one more completion. On SMP that CPU time is largely CPU1's and already free, so expect 0-3% fps; it matters most on UP, under background load, and for the worst-frame tail. It also removes the last CPU pixel loop from the fullscreen path, which is the structurally interesting part.
rule_check: Our compositor and our driver; no app change, no upstream patch, nothing disabled. RAM cost is neutral (the index plane moves from malloc to GEM, same size) and the buffer comes from CMA, which is sized already.
prior_attempts: PPA CLUT lost three times windowed (-7.5% at 320x200, parity at 640x400, -4% under adaptive dispatch, 29.6 vs 30.5 from a copied GEM plane) and the register's own reading of why is the bounce copy and the flush, both of which this form removes. 'Offload isn't purchasable below ~128 KB' argues against the 77 KB op in isolation; chaining it to an op the driver already submits is what may cross that line. Lowest-confidence item here; it should only be built if the sweep's cheaper items are exhausted.

title: Symbolise the user side of the hart0 PC sampler, at instruction granularity — 24% of the machine is five pixel loops and the samples pile on their load/store
layer: instrumentation (scripts/board/h1s-report.py + a maps/PID capture in the runsh arming script; no board change needed to start)
mechanism: The hart0 PC sampler reads hart1's PC from the bus monitor (0x2d0020d0) and h1s-report.py resolves it against System.map — kernel symbols only. Everything below 0xC0000000 is bucketed as 'user: the program itself' / 'user: shared libraries' by a fixed 0x80000000 address split and never named. That is 58.7% of the machine reported as two anonymous numbers. The fix is small: have the arming script also cat /proc/<pid>/maps for the workload (and, for exactness, have the kernel store current->pid in an uncached SRAM word on context switch so the sampler records (PC,PID) pairs — two stores in __switch_to), then resolve each user PC against the right ELF's symbol table. Second, and this is the part with no cost at all: report the histogram WITHIN a hot function at instruction granularity. The bus monitor samples the pipeline PC, so a hart stalled on a cache miss keeps reporting the same PC — sample mass piles up on the instruction adjacent to whatever is stalling. I ran both offline against the existing capture artifacts/quake/h1s-062518/pcs.txt with rootfs/tiopex-quake.dbg (PIE base recovered by symbol-coverage search, 0x6909e000, 5,916 of 5,950 samples resolved).
evidence: Recovered user profile, share of ALL 12,000 samples: D_DrawSpans8 11.90%, D_DrawZSpans 4.62%, R_RenderView_ 2.95%, __muldf3 2.57%, R_DrawSurfaceBlock8_mip0 2.39%, D_PolysetDrawSpans8 2.07%, R_RecursiveWorldNode 1.64%, R_LeadingEdge 1.61%, R_DrawSurfaceBlock8_mip1 1.52%. The ten pixel-writing inner loops sum to 23.98% of the machine.

Instruction-level: D_DrawZSpans has 53.4% of its samples on ONE offset, +0x100 (0x16c76, the `or` immediately before `sw a5,0(a3)` — the z-buffer store) and 71% inside the 8-instruction inner loop 0x16c6a-0x16c7e. D_DrawSpans8 has 19.5% on +0x1dc (the loop branch, right after `sb a5,-1(a4)`) and 13.7% on +0x1d2 (the `add` right before `lbu a5,0(a5)`, the texel fetch) — 33% of the function on the two instructions bracketing its load and its store. R_DrawSurfaceBlock8_mip0: 34.5% on one offset.

Arithmetic on D_DrawZSpans: 4.62% of a 58.5 ms frame = 2.70 ms/frame; its inner loop is 8 instructions per 2 z-pixels, so ~60k z-pixels/frame is ~240k instructions = 0.75 ms at IPC 1 and 320 MHz. Implied CPI ~3.6, i.e. ~70% of that function is stall. Same shape for D_DrawSpans8.

Soft-double helpers inside the app total 4.10% of the machine (__muldf3 2.57, __extendsfdf2 0.45, __fixdfsi 0.28, __gtdf2/__adddf3/__divdf3/__ltdf2/__subdf3 the rest). App-internal, so unfixable under the rules — but it is a bound nobody had, and it sets the ceiling on any Quake work.

The library side cannot be attributed at all today: one 404 KB mapping at 0x95730000-0x95794fff holds 761 samples = 6.34% of the machine. I tried to name it by symbol-coverage search against libc.so (dynamic symbols) and the unstripped libSDL-1.2.so.0.11.4 from the container; both produced nonsense (regcomp, sem_open, csqrt in a Quake timedemo). Without /proc/pid/maps it is unnameable, and 6.34% of the machine is in code we are allowed to change (musl, SDL1.2, libasound).
docs/smp-finish-plan.md:145-146 is the whole of what the review knows today: 'user 59% (program 51, libs 8)'. Nothing below that line exists.
The sampler cannot currently tell Quake from lvdesk from any other process — both are PIE and land in overlapping ranges. The 50.9% 'the program itself' is an assumption, not a measurement.
magnitude_estimate: Instrument, not a win. It reframes 58.7% of the machine that is currently two anonymous numbers, and it has already produced one concrete finding: 24% of the machine is in five loops whose sample mass sits on a single load or store each, with implied CPI ~3.6. If that stall reading holds, ~15-17% of the machine is waiting on PSRAM inside code we cannot touch — which makes the memory system, not the code, the target. It also names the 6.3% library mapping, which IS ours to change. Cost: ~50 lines of Python plus one `cat /proc/<pid>/maps` in the arming script; zero extra board time, and the existing captures can be re-reported offline today.
rule_check: Clean. Read-only observation of an unmodified app; the app binary is not rebuilt, relinked or steered — rootfs/tiopex-quake.dbg is the same build with symbols kept alongside. The optional PID-tag word is a two-store kernel change on the platform side. No flash, no Bluetooth/Wi-Fi disabled, no upstream patching, no RAM cost (the SRAM tag word is 4 bytes).
prior_attempts: h1s + h1s-report.py exist and have been used four times (artifacts/quake/h1s-062518, h1s-tyr.txt, h1s-tyr2.txt) but have only ever resolved kernel symbols. The dead-end register's 'libc mem* is 0.73% of Quake's CPU0' and 'all non-libc shared libraries are 1.4%' come from 'lens:libs objdump' — static reasoning, not from this profile, and they are inconsistent with 6.34% sitting in one unidentified mapping. The instruction-level view has never been taken; the docstring's own advertised use (symbol-by-symbol UP vs SMP comparison) was never exercised either.

title: Count retired instructions: instret is available and unused, so nothing on this board has ever measured CPI — the predictor that would have killed three .text..fast picks before they were built
layer: kernel (arch/riscv, one CSR write + a per-tick ring) and a user probe
mechanism: The hart reports zicntr, so cycle/time/instret exist. OpenSBI already sets mcounteren = -1 (opensbi-esp32-s31/lib/sbi/sbi_hart.c:74), so S-mode can read instret TODAY with no change at all. Linux sets scounteren = 0x2 (head.S:169 and :302 — TM only), so U-mode gets rdtime but not rdcycle/rdinstret; making it 0x7 is a one-line platform change. timebase-frequency is 320000000 (esp32s31.dtsi:196), the core clock, so rdtime already counts at cycle resolution — the only missing quantity in the whole machine is the instruction count. Instrument: (a) a tick-rate (cycle, instret, pt_regs->epc) ring in the timer handler gives a per-PC CPI map — for each sampled PC region, cycles spent against instructions retired; (b) a trivial user probe brackets a region and reports its CPI directly. Two numbers per sample, no new hardware, no perf, no ftrace. Validate first (the 'silent instrument' rule): confirm instret is real and is not tied to zero or aliased to cycle, by running a known-length loop out of internal SRAM and checking instret against the static instruction count.
evidence: scounteren = 0x2 at linux-71-port/arch/riscv/kernel/head.S:169,302; mcounteren = -1 at opensbi-esp32-s31/lib/sbi/sbi_hart.c:74. So S-mode instret works now; U-mode needs one line.

lvdesk already proved the CSR route works from U-mode for rdtime and that it is worth doing: lvdesk/lvdesk.c:4295-4320 records that clock_gettime was 16.4% of lvdesk's on-CPU samples before the CSR replaced it. The same probe pattern (SIGILL-guarded) applies to instret.

The .text..fast programme has been selecting candidates by PC-sample share, and that predictor has failed repeatedly: input+evdev +3.8%, irq/chip.o <1% despite being ~0.8% of CPU0, DRM commit 26.8 kB gave 5095 vs 5146 us (<1%), sbitmap/blk-mq-tag nothing, rcu/tree.o -1.7%/+4%, while softirq.o alone gave -19.7%. Sample share does not distinguish 'slow because it refetches from flash' from 'slow because it waits on PSRAM' — CPI does. Flash-fetch stall shows as high CPI that collapses when the object moves; PSRAM data stall shows as high CPI that does not.

The budget this would rank: 28.4% of the machine executes kernel FLASH text and 11.8% already executes from .text..fast RAM (recomputed from artifacts/quake/h1s-062518 against images/System.map). Subtracting arch_cpu_idle (8.6%, a WFI loop where fetch cost is irrelevant) leaves 19.8% of the machine still fetching kernel code from 80 MHz flash, against a 16 KB I-cache and a measured 5.98x RAM-vs-flash ratio for straight-line code.
There is no per-object measurement of I-cache behaviour anywhere in docs/ or the dead-end register; hot-text-plan.md and the .lds.S comments rank by profile share only.
magnitude_estimate: Instrument. It puts a number on the 19.8% of the machine still fetching kernel text from flash and says which of it is actually paying the 6x — the difference between a 3.8% win and a <1% one, which the current selection method cannot see in advance. Each wrong .text..fast pick has cost a build plus 3-4 boots of measurement (the 10-minute rule) and burns scarce RAM budget and shared D-cache. It also gives the direct test of the stall hypothesis in proposal 1: CPI inside D_DrawSpans8/D_DrawZSpans, measured rather than inferred.
rule_check: Clean. Kernel-side only; the app is untouched and unaware. Cost is one CSR write plus a small per-CPU ring (a few KB, sized by the caller) — trivial against 15.4 MB. No effect on Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or any feature. No upstream code patched.
prior_attempts: Never tried. The dead-end register's 'there is no perf, no ftrace, no PMU' has been read as 'no counters at all'; it is only true of zihpm event counters, which this hart does not list. zicntr's instret was overlooked. docs/current-state.md:905-936 measured syscall costs with clock_gettime and concluded the syscall tax was <0.5%, but never asked what the cycles it did find were spent on.

title: Dump the D-cache tag array: nobody knows how the shared 64 KB is divided between Quake, the kernel, lvdesk and hart0's firmware, and the cache is physically indexed so page placement is a live per-boot variable
layer: hart0 loader firmware (bootloader/main, alongside the existing PC sampler) + an offline resolver
mechanism: The cache block exposes its tag and data memories to software: CACHE_L1_CACHE_OBJECT_CTRL selects the object (CACHE_L1_DCACHE_TAG_OBJECT bit 4, ICACHE0..3 tag at bits 0-3, the matching MEM_OBJECT bits at 6-10), CACHE_L1_CACHE_WAY_OBJECT picks the way (3 bits, so up to 8), CACHE_L1_CACHE_ADDR picks the index, and CACHE_L1_CACHE_DEBUG_BUS reads the value; CACHE_L1_CACHE_FREEZE_CTRL freezes allocation so the snapshot is coherent. 64 KB of 64 B lines is 1,024 tag reads — under a millisecond. Run it from hart0 exactly like the PC sampler (same control-word handshake, same internal-SRAM buffer), take 50-100 snapshots through a timedemo, and resolve each tag to an owner: Quake's buffers via /proc/<pid>/pagemap for its VMAs, the kernel via its physical map, hart0's FreeRTOS/Wi-Fi/BT heaps via the loader's nm output. Output: a census of who holds the shared cache, and a per-set occupancy histogram. The same block also carries the bus monitor's AREA windows (BUS_MONITOR_CORE_x_AREA_DRAM0_0/1 and AREA_PIF_0/1 MIN/MAX with RD_ENA/WR_ENA/RAW and an AREA_PC capture register) as a second channel for attributing traffic, not just occupancy, to an address range plus the PC that touched it.
evidence: Register set confirmed in the container: /opt/esp-idf/components/soc/esp32s31/register/soc/cache_reg.h — OBJECT_CTRL at DR_REG_CACHE_BASE+0x260, WAY_OBJECT +0x264 (bitpos [2:0]), ADDR +0x268, DEBUG_BUS +0x26c ('a constant place where we can write data to or read data from the tag/data memory on the specified cache'), plus FREEZE_CTRL, TAG_MEM_ACS_CONF and DATA_MEM_ACS_CONF.

This is a memory-side cache shared by both harts, not a core-private one: CACHE_L1_DCACHE_CTRL carries SHUT_DBUS0..3 bits and the counters are per master (L1_DBUS0..3 and L1_IBUS0..3 ACS_HIT/MISS/CONFLICT/NXTLVL_RD/NXTLVL_WR). It is therefore physically indexed and tagged, so which physical frames the kernel hands Quake decides which cache sets its buffers land in.

Geometry makes that load-bearing: 64 KB / 64 B = 1,024 lines; at 8 ways that is 128 sets and index bits [12:6], one bit above the 4 KiB page boundary. Physical page placement changes the set for half of every buffer.

This is a candidate mechanism for the per-boot lottery that has never been tested. The eliminations so far (worklog-2026-09-19.md:1609-1767) are all runtime: not placement, not an lvdesk restart, not the scanout buffer address, not CMA, not PSRAM chase latency, not Quake paging. 'A reset leaves slow boots slow' is exactly what a boot-fixed physical-layout effect looks like, because the free-page layout a demo allocates from is set by how the boot went.

The dead-end register records the constraint that makes this matter: 'RAM text costs shared D-cache' is the stated reason #337 (chip.o in .text..fast) was not shipped, and 'Hardware that is not available' closes the cache geometry as fixed — but nobody has looked at what is in it.
Every candidate that moves bytes into cached PSRAM (.text..fast, hot userspace text, RAM copies of hot data) is priced against a cache whose current occupants are unknown.
magnitude_estimate: Instrument. Three things it would size, none of which has a number today: (1) how much of the shared 64 KB hart0's firmware and radios hold while Quake runs — if it is a third, moving hart0's hot data into internal SRAM (which does not go through this cache) is a direct recovery and a platform-side change we are allowed to make; (2) whether the 24% of the machine in Quake's pixel loops is losing lines to conflict misses rather than capacity misses, which page-colouring the anon allocator could address; (3) whether the +-10% per-boot lottery is a physical-layout aliasing effect, which would retire the largest single source of noise in the whole project and is the precondition for trusting any result under 10%.
rule_check: Clean, with one caveat to measure: FREEZE_CTRL stalls allocation for the ~1 ms of a snapshot, so the instrument perturbs hart1 and must be measured against itself (take snapshots at 1 Hz and at 10 Hz and check the timedemo result does not move). App untouched, no flash writes beyond a loader build, no feature disabled, no upstream code patched, no RAM cost (1,024 words of internal SRAM, and the existing sampler already owns 16 KB there).
prior_attempts: Never tried. The dead-end register covers cache CONFIGURATION ('Enlarge or reconfigure the caches from the loader' — not available, geometry fixed) and the autoload/prelock knobs, but not cache INSPECTION. The related round-1 proposal 'use the l1 cache access counters' asks for hit/miss RATES; this asks who is in the cache and in which sets, which the counters cannot answer.

title: Measure memory-level parallelism: the 102 / 192 / 210 MB/s numbers all fall out of one serialised 64-byte transfer at ~310 ns, which would mean the CPU never overlaps a miss — and that gates every prefetch idea on the list
layer: userspace microbenchmark (rootfs/, alongside membw) plus a kernel-side control
mechanism: Three of the platform's headline constants are consistent with a memory path that has exactly one outstanding transfer. 64 B at ~310 ns is 206 MB/s: a CPU fill (one transfer per line) measures 192 MB/s; a CPU copy (a read line plus a write line, serialised) predicts 103 MB/s and measures 102; GDMA, which can overlap, measures 210. The recorded dependent-chase latency is 275-316 ns, the same number. If that model is right the CPU has zero memory-level parallelism and every cache miss costs the full latency with nothing hidden behind it — which explains proposal 1's stall pile-ups and, more importantly, decides whether the D-cache autoload/preload sections are worth anything. The probe is small and decisive: at a fixed footprint well outside 64 KB, compare (a) a dependent pointer chase, (b) N independent strided loads per iteration for N = 1,2,4,8, (c) the same for stores. If per-access time is flat in N, MLP is 1 and no software restructuring of our libraries can hide a miss; if it falls, MLP is N and the autoload sections (CACHE_L1_DCACHE_AUTOLOAD_SCT0..3, each an address plus a size) become a real lever that the kernel could point at a VMA. Run it on hart1 alone and again with hart0 loaded, to get the contended figure as well.
evidence: The constants that fit the model, all from the task's own measured set: PSRAM copy ~102 MB/s CPU, fill 192, GDMA 210, PPA 153; dependent chase 275-316 ns (worklog-2026-09-19.md:1609-1767, where a slow boot read 274.8 ns and fast boots 316 ns).
64 B / 310 ns = 206 MB/s single transfer; x2 for a copy = 103 MB/s. The agreement with 102 and 192 is close enough to be worth testing and too close to ignore.

At 320 MHz, 310 ns is ~99 cycles per miss. The implied CPI ~3.6 in D_DrawZSpans (proposal 1) needs roughly one unoverlapped miss per 3-4 loop iterations, which is exactly what a 150 KB streaming z-buffer write through a 64 KB cache produces at 64 B per line.

The dead-end register shows the prefetch family has only ever been attacked from the configuration side, never sized: I-cache autoload from Linux killed the hart twice and from the loader was a no-op because the flag only applies when the cache is disabled. The DCACHE autoload sections (four of them, with address and size registers) have never been touched at all.

docs memory note s31-write-combine-streams is the nearest prior art and points the same way: 'WC has few fill buffers: one sequential stream uses them perfectly, three evict each other on every access' — 1 stream 1.0x, 3 streams 18x. That is a statement about how few outstanding transfers this memory path supports, made about write-combine mappings; nobody asked the same question of the cached path.
magnitude_estimate: Instrument, and a gate. If MLP is 1, it retires the whole prefetch/autoload family for the CPU path in one afternoon (nothing can be overlapped, so nothing can be prefetched into use in time) and redirects the effort at reducing miss COUNT — fewer streams, better placement, smaller working sets. If MLP is 2-4, then the four DCACHE autoload sections applied to the streaming z-buffer and screen-buffer writes could approach the GDMA figure (210 vs 102 MB/s, ~2x) on the write side of the 24% of the machine in pixel loops, which would be the first double-digit candidate found in this review. Either answer is worth a day.
rule_check: Clean. A read-only microbenchmark in rootfs/ next to membw; the app is untouched and this does not run while a game does. No flash, no feature disabled, no upstream patching, negligible RAM. Must follow the measurement rules: fresh boot per arm, 5+ repeats, report the spread — the per-boot lottery is larger than the effect sizes the probe is looking for in the contended case.
prior_attempts: Never measured. 'PSRAM chase latency' was measured once (275-316 ns) purely to test the per-boot lottery and was recorded as an elimination, not as a memory-system characterisation; the dependent case is the only one that has ever been run. docs/accel-plan.md compares engines by throughput without a latency/parallelism model behind the numbers.

title: Profile the whole run, tagged by frame and by process: the tail and the +-10% per-boot lottery have been counted many times and never once profiled
layer: hart0 loader firmware (extend the existing H1 PC SAMPLER) + resolver
mechanism: The sampler is capped at 4,000 samples in internal SRAM at 1 kHz — four seconds, taken as three windows mid-demo, out of a 56.6 s run. Everything the complaint is actually about happens outside that window: the p99 dips and the boot-to-boot swing. Two changes make it a whole-run instrument. First, spill the ring into PSRAM (hart0 can write it; the existing SRAM control word stays as the handshake, since the note in s31_vcpu.c records that a PSRAM control word sat in hart1's D-cache and was never seen) — 56,000 samples is 224 KB, drained after the run. Second, record a second word per sample: a tag that software writes to a fixed uncached SRAM location. lvdesk stamps its present counter there (it already keeps one for frame-gap tracking), and the kernel stamps current->pid on context switch. That yields (PC, frame, pid) triples. Then: diff the slowest 5% of frames against the median frame, symbol by symbol; and diff a fast boot against a slow boot, symbol by symbol, which is the comparison h1s-report.py's own docstring advertises and which has never been run.
evidence: The current capture is three 4 s windows inside a 56.6 s demo: artifacts/quake/h1s-062518/run.sh runs `for k in 1 2 3; do /root/h1s ... 4000; sleep 4; done` after `sleep 25`. Buffer limit is hard-coded: `volatile uint32_t s31_h1s_buf[4000]` in bootloader/main/s31_vcpu.c, 1 kHz from an esp_timer.

The dips have been characterised only statistically and negatively: 'Dips are CPU contention (no positional correlation, r=0.04-0.33; half the slow intervals had zero faults)'. No profile of a dip exists. The p99 dip block was unchanged by XLITE-RING and by fast present (0.692 -> 0.709 s), which is what you expect when the cause has never been identified.

The lottery is the largest effect in the project and is unexplained: 17.3, 17.1, 14.4, 16.2 fps on fresh boots of the same image (docs/smp-finish-plan.md:161-165). smp-finish-plan says in bold 'Fix the boot lottery first... until it is found every SMP number carries a 17% lottery'. Six mechanisms have been eliminated; none was eliminated by looking at what the CPU was doing differently.
The sampler cannot currently attribute a sample to a process at all, so even 'is the slow boot slow inside Quake or inside the kernel' is unanswered. The PID tag is two stores in __switch_to.
The profile as it stands is extremely flat — 400 distinct kernel symbols, top one 0.78% — which is exactly the shape that hides a cost that only appears in 5% of frames.
magnitude_estimate: Instrument. It targets the two largest unexplained quantities on the board: a +-10% boot-to-boot swing that is bigger than every lever ever shipped, and a p99 tail that is the actual user complaint (the docs' own rule is 'watch the tail, not the median'). It does not itself win anything, but no result under 10% can be believed until the lottery is understood, so it is on the critical path for every remaining candidate. Cost: ~40 lines in the loader, two stores in the kernel, one resolver change; the capture itself costs hart1 nothing.
rule_check: Clean. hart0 already runs the sampler timer and is 64% idle during Quake, so the cost lands on the lent hart, not on CPU0. 224 KB of PSRAM for the ring is real but transient and only allocated when profiling. App untouched. No feature disabled, no upstream patching. Board time respects the 10-minute rule: one boot per capture, 3-4 boots per comparison.
prior_attempts: The sampler was built on 2026-09-21 and used as-is four times. The lottery work (worklog-2026-09-19.md:1609-1767) eliminated placement, lvdesk restart, scanout address, CMA, PSRAM chase latency and paging, all without ever taking a profile on a slow boot. dip-analyse.py and dipwatch.sh count dips and correlate them with faults; neither says what ran.

title: The kernel already knows how to satisfy N contiguous swap entries with ONE SD request — two gates that have nothing to do with this board keep it off, and every swap-in is a lone 4 KiB read
layer: Kernel mm: do_swap_page / swapin_readahead (mm/memory.c, mm/swap_state.c); optionally drivers/mmc block queue limits
mechanism:
Upstream 7.1 contains exactly the mechanism this board needs. `can_swapin_thp()` (mm/memory.c:4637) tests whether an aligned run of PTEs are all swap entries with *consecutive* swap offsets (via `swap_pte_batch()`, mm/internal.h:450), all non-zeromap and all out of the swapcache; `alloc_swap_folio()` (mm/memory.c:4690) then allocates one folio covering the whole run and `swapin_folio()` reads it in a single I/O. On this board it is unreachable twice over. (1) mm/memory.c:4878 only takes that path when the swap device has `SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO`, set at mm/swapfile.c:3561 from `bdev_synchronous()`; the only drivers in the tree that set `BLK_FEAT_SYNCHRONOUS` are brd.c:312 and zram_drv.c:3048 — mmc never does, so our /swapfile always takes the `swapin_readahead()` branch at mm/memory.c:4891. (2) `alloc_swap_folio()` degenerates to the order-0 stub at mm/memory.c:4770 because `CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE` is off, and arch/riscv/Kconfig:148 selects `HAVE_ARCH_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE` only `if 64BIT && MMU`. Result: on rv32 every major fault is exactly one 4 KiB bio, and the board pays the flat ~2.49 ms SD request floor 1,296 times per demo to move 5.3 MB.

The proposal is to implement the order-0 equivalent, which needs neither THP nor the synchronous-queue flag. In `swapin_readahead()`, before choosing a readahead mode, run `swap_pte_batch()` outward from the faulting PTE (clamped to the PMD and to 16 pages). If it finds a run of R>1 PTEs holding consecutive offsets, allocate R order-0 folios into the swapcache, add them to ONE bio (a bio carries scattered pages for contiguous sectors — that is what it is for), submit under the existing plug, wait only for the target, and let the other R-1 be claimed by the minor faults that follow within microseconds. Cost model: R pages in one request is 2.49 + R*4KiB/48MB/s ms instead of R*2.49 ms — 16 pages for 3.8 ms instead of 39.8 ms.

This is categorically not the page-cluster arms that failed. `swap_cluster_readahead()` (mm/swap_state.c:698) reads *physical* neighbours with no check that they belong to this VMA or this address neighbourhood, allocates them as speculative folios and pushes them onto the LRU (`lru_add_drain()`, mm/swap_state.c:742) — at ~316 kB free every speculative page evicts a real one, which is why page-cluster 3 made the Quake demo not finish. Here the extra pages pass a triple-adjacency test (same VMA, consecutive virtual addresses, consecutive swap slots) and are mapped into the page table immediately; nothing is fetched that the process has not already demonstrably swapped out as one contiguous run.

title: Swap slots are handed out in reclaim order, so the 10 MB Quake heap's image on the card refragments every cycle — allocate them by virtual address instead and adjacency becomes a property, not luck
layer: Kernel mm: swap slot allocator (mm/swapfile.c folio_alloc_swap / swap_alloc_fast / cluster_alloc_swap_entry)
mechanism:
Every swap slot on this board comes from a per-CPU cluster scanned linearly: `folio_alloc_swap()` (mm/swapfile.c:1696) -> `swap_alloc_fast()` (1349) takes `this_cpu_read(percpu_swap_cluster...)` and `alloc_swap_scan_cluster()` walks it, falling back to `cluster_alloc_swap_entry()` (1074). So slot order == the order pages came off the LRU == reclaim order. During Quake's load phase that happens to be roughly address order (the hunk is filled linearly), but across 58.5 s with ~5.3 MB cycling in and out, and with two CPUs each holding their own cluster, the correspondence decays into access order and the free-slot map fragments. That is why every readahead scheme measured here has had to *guess*.

For private anonymous memory the information to do better is already in hand at allocation time: an anon folio's `->index` is its linear page index within the VMA, and `folio_anon_vma(folio)` identifies the mapping. Proposal: on the first swap-out from a private anon VMA above a threshold (say 1 MB), reserve a contiguous run of `vma_pages(vma)` swap offsets and thereafter allocate `slot = base + folio->index`, falling back to the stock allocator when no reservation exists, when the folio is shared, or when the target slot is occupied. Release the run on VMA teardown. The 64 MB swapfile (etc/init.d/S04s31-swap, SIZE_MB=64, dd'd so ext4 gives it few extents and `iomap_swapfile_activate` maps it near-contiguously on the card) has room for a 10 MB VMA several times over; SWAPFILE_CLUSTER is 256 pages (mm/swap.h:15), so a 2,560-page reservation is ten clusters.

What it buys: virtual adjacency and slot adjacency become the same thing, permanently and idempotently. `can_swapin_thp`-style run detection (proposal 1) then always finds the full neighbourhood instead of whatever survived the last reclaim pass; physical-slot readahead becomes precise rather than speculative; and swap-out writes from `shrink_lruvec`'s plug (mm/vmscan.c:5955) merge into large sequential requests by construction, which matters most during the launch phase that pushes ~7.4 MB out. It also makes the card image of the heap stable across cycles, so a page swapped out, in, and out again lands back on the same sectors.

title: Put a small raw chunk cache in front of the swapfile — the one form of swap readahead whose RAM cost is fixed and that never touches the LRU
layer: Kernel mm: swap read path (mm/page_io.c swap_read_folio_bdev_async / swap_read_folio), with invalidation hooks in swap_entry_free / swap_writepage
mechanism:
Every readahead experiment on this board failed the same way: a speculative page becomes a real folio in the swapcache and on the LRU (`lru_add_drain()` at mm/swap_state.c:742), so at ~316 kB free each one evicts a page somebody wanted, and the amplification is unbounded because the window scales with the fault rate. That is the mechanism behind page-cluster 3 not finishing the demo, and it is the same mechanism that sank zram four times (etc/s31-swap.conf: 'a compressed copy of RAM in RAM is not a saving here').

A raw chunk cache dodges all of it. Reserve a fixed N (128-512 KiB) of kernel memory as aligned chunks of the swapfile's *block* image. On a swap-in for offset X that misses, issue one read of the aligned chunk containing X (one 64-256 KiB SD request, 3.8-8.0 ms), serve X by memcpy into the newly allocated folio (4 KiB at ~102 MB/s = ~40 us) and keep the rest of the chunk. Every later fault landing inside a held chunk costs ~40 us instead of ~2,490 us — a 60x reduction with no folio allocation, no swapcache insert, no LRU entry and no reclaim triggered. Invalidate a chunk when any slot inside it is freed or rewritten (`swap_entry_free`, `swap_writepage`); keep it read-only so there is no writeback coherence problem at all.

The key difference from readahead is that the memory cost is a constant chosen by us, not a function of the fault rate, so the failure mode that has killed every previous attempt cannot occur: the cache never grows, never competes for the LRU, and never forces an eviction beyond the N bytes it was given at boot. This composes with proposal 2 — with address-ordered slots a 256 KiB chunk is 256 KiB of contiguous hunk, which is a model, a texture set or a BSP region, exactly the granularity at which Quake touches the heap.
