RAM is the binding constraint and this proposal spends a fixed, explicitly chosen amount of it — the honest accounting is that N bytes of cache is N bytes more swap, and the proposal is only worth shipping if the measured hit rate beats that.
prior_attempts: Not tried in this form. Every previous attempt to make paging cheaper by spending RAM (zram at 24 MB, 4 MB, and 512 kB mem_limit; page-cluster 0/3/5; readahead 16-1024 kB) spent it as *pages on the LRU*, where the cost grows with pressure. A fixed raw block cache has never been built here. The dead-end register's 'CPU1 prefetch daemon: no predictor at 316 kB free' rejects a different thing — a predictor — and the free-memory half of that objection is exactly what a fixed-size cache answers.

title: musl is platform code, and it is where the 10 MB Quake heap's backing store is chosen — a huge malloc could be a file mapping instead of anonymous memory
layer: musl libc (shared libc.so the apps load dynamically) — malloc's large-allocation path
mechanism:
The task's standing question is whether the 10 MB heap could be backed differently without touching the app. It can, and the place to do it is not the kernel: TyrQuake's `-mem 10` is one `malloc(10485760)`, musl's mallocng serves that with a direct `mmap(MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS)`, and everything downstream — swap slots, page-cluster, the swapcache — follows from that single flag choice. The hard rules explicitly put 'musl libc/ld.so' on the platform side.

Proposal: in musl's large-allocation path, above a threshold (4 MB, so only a game-sized heap qualifies), create an unlinked file on the writable root, write it out to real extents (not `fallocate`, which leaves unwritten extents that fault-time allocation can turn into SIGBUS under ENOSPC), `mmap(MAP_SHARED, fd)` it, and remember the fd for free()/munmap. The heap then leaves the swap subsystem entirely and joins the filesystem path: faults go through `filemap_fault` with the block device's adaptive `ondemand_readahead` and a 128 KiB window instead of swap's fixed `page_cluster`; writeback is done by the flusher thread in large contiguous bios instead of per-folio swap writes; and pages that are written once at load and only read thereafter become *clean* file pages, droppable with no I/O at all.

Three things must be handled or it will not work, and they are the reason to treat this as a one-boot experiment rather than a plan. (a) `MMAP_LOTSAMISS` (mm/filemap.c:3258) turns mmap read-around off entirely once a file has missed 100 times more than it hit (mm/filemap.c:3346-3357), which under thrash is immediate — so musl must also `madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL)` on the region to set VM_SEQ_READ, which takes the unconditional `page_cache_sync_ra(ra->ra_pages)` branch. (b) file pages sit on the file LRU, and `vm.swappiness = 10` ships precisely to make the kernel throw file pages away first, so without revisiting that the heap would be evicted harder than it is today. (c) mmap writes are subject to dirty throttling, which anonymous memory is not, so the load phase could be rate-limited by `vm.dirty_ratio` on a machine whose dirty limit is ~1.5 MB.

The dead-end register covers XIP for library text, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, lazy PLT binding, -Bsymbolic-functions and XEspV mem* in musl — all about musl's *text*, none about where malloc puts a multi-megabyte allocation. 'Game config/binary changes (-mem 12/10/9)' varied the heap's *size* from the app side and found 9.8/10.9/10.1 fps, non-monotonic; this varies its *backing* from the platform side, which is a different variable and is the one the rules still allow.

title: The xlite ring doorbell threw away the scheduler hint the socket carried: eventfd wakes are not sync wakes
layer: xlite/xshim transport (userspace), optionally one line in fs/eventfd.c
mechanism: XLITE-RING replaced the af_unix socket with two eventfd doorbells. Every socket wake in Linux is a *sync* wake (sock_def_readable uses wake_up_interruptible_sync_poll), and so is every pipe wake; eventfd_write is the odd one out, using wake_up_locked_poll with wake_flags 0. In 7.1 WF_SYNC drives two separate decisions: wake_affine_idle() returns the waker's CPU when the waker's runqueue has exactly one runnable task (i.e. the waker is about to block, which is precisely what Quake does after ShmPutImage+XSync), and preempt_sync() suppresses the immediate preemption of the waker by the wakee. Without the hint, each frame's doorbell is free to migrate the peer to the other hart (a 165 us crossing plus an emulated interrupt entry on the lent CPU) and/or to preempt the game mid-frame and cost it a context switch out of its slice. The hint propagates through poll(): fs/select.c __pollwake passes `sync` into default_wake_function, so a reader blocked in poll() on a *pipe* gets WF_SYNC while a reader blocked on an *eventfd* never can. Fix without touching the kernel: make the doorbell a pipe pair instead of an eventfd (same poll set, same drain-then-clear-sig protocol, one extra fd per direction), behind XLITE_RING_PIPE=1 so it is a warm-board A/B. A 1-line kernel variant (sync wake in eventfd_write) exists if the pipe write turns out dearer than the eventfd write.

title: Cut the compositor's frame at the point where the client stops waiting, and give the second half its own thread
layer: lvdesk/xshim
mechanism: The per-frame compositor work is two units with opposite scheduling requirements welded into one poll loop. Unit A (ShmPutImage: copy+row-hash 76.8 kB out of the client's segment, xshim.c:5489-5550) is what the client's XSync waits for; it belongs next to the client and is on the critical path. Unit B (late_present_drain -> fs_present: a second full-frame row hash, the palette expand into the 320x240 mode framebuffer, the cache flush, the PRESENT ioctl and the PPA dispatch, 3-5 ms) is off the critical path BY CONSTRUCTION — that is what late present established — and must never run on the game's CPU. Today one thread does both, so the scheduler is asked one placement question for two contradictory jobs and whichever way it answers, one of them is wrong; placement is currently decided by luck (measured: 'lvdesk ~30% of a core, mostly on CPU1'). Give unit B its own thread with its own queue and let the stock scheduler place it. Rider: unit A already computes the exact per-row changed bitmap (xshim.c:5540-5545, b->rowhash[ty] != hv) and unit B throws it away and hashes the same 76.8 kB again (lvdesk.c fs_present, fsrh_hash); hand the bitmap across the split and one full-frame hash pass per frame disappears for free.
evidence: docs/worklog-2026-09-21-latepresent.md — late present = +13% on Doom (34.6 -> 39.1 fps), frames under 25 ms 1219 -> 2626, 50-100 ms stutters 74 -> 39: proof that the serialization and not the work was the cost

Built kernel .config: CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS, CONFIG_SCHED_INFO, CONFIG_TASKSTATS and CONFIG_PSI are all off, so /proc/<tid>/schedstat does not exist and no runqueue-wait figure has ever been taken
magnitude_estimate: 3-5 ms per frame of unit-B work kept off the game's CPU: 50-85 ms/s at Quake's 17 fps (5-8% of a core) and 120-200 ms/s at Doom's 39 fps, plus ~1 ms/frame from dropping the duplicate hash, minus one thread wake per frame (~0.3-0.5 ms). Net estimate 4-8% on Quake, 5-10% on Doom. Cost side is one thread stack and one queue.

prior_attempts: The 2026-09-21 survey concluded 'no thread to add and no thread needed: lvdesk is one poll() loop' — but that survey ran BEFORE late present existed, i.e. when there genuinely was nothing to overlap, and late present then disproved its premise. This is not affinity policy (forced placement, capacity-dmips and RPS/workqueue steering all measured worse); it makes the work separable so the stock scheduler can do its job, which is the project's own stated principle 1.

title: There is no instrument on this board that can see runqueue wait, and the 20 fps goal's arithmetic depends on one
layer: kernel config (diagnostic build) + measurement method
mechanism: The stated ceiling for the whole goal — 'the ceiling is removing Quake's waits: 17.3 / 0.84 = 20.6 fps' — comes from waitsamp, which classifies a thread by /proc/<tid>/stat state. TASK_RUNNING prints 'R' whether the thread is ON a CPU or merely QUEUED behind another task, so waitsamp's 'running 86%' is 'running or waiting for a CPU', and its residual 14% ('short sleeps ~10%', ppoll 1.8%, faults ~2%) is only the blocked part. If a slice of the 86% is runqueue wait, the ceiling is higher than 20.6 fps and the fix is placement (proposals 1 and 2); if it is not, the fix must be throughput and the whole 20 fps target needs 16% more Quake work per second. These have opposite remedies and nothing currently distinguishes them: CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS, CONFIG_SCHED_INFO, CONFIG_TASKSTATS and CONFIG_PSI are all off in the built kernel, so /proc/<tid>/schedstat is not even created, and there is no perf and no ftrace. Build one diagnostic kernel with CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS=y (it selects SCHED_INFO; it adds three u64 per task and a couple of timestamp updates per switch, no debugfs, so it does not bring back the 1.14 MB DEBUG_FS cost) and read run_delay and pcount for Quake's main thread, lvdesk and the SDL audio thread over a timedemo.
evidence: docs/smp-finish-plan.md 'Quake, where CPU0 goes and what it waits on (2026-09-22)' — 'waitsamp: running 86%'; 'The ceiling is removing Quake's waits: 17.3 / 0.84 = 20.6 fps'
rootfs/waitsamp.c:1-18 — 'Running samples are counted as "R"'; it reads /proc/<tid>/stat, /wchan and /syscall at a 5 ms period, which is coarser than the sleeps it is trying to name
Built kernel .config (read via docker/build.sh): '# CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS is not set', '# CONFIG_TASKSTATS is not set', '# CONFIG_PSI is not set', CONFIG_SCHED_INFO absent
linux-71-port/fs/proc/base.c:504,3344,3688 — the schedstat file is guarded by CONFIG_SCHED_INFO, so it does not exist today
CPU0 profile: user 59%, kernel 32%, idle 9%, of which scheduler 5.1% + timers/clock 4.8% + IRQ/CLIC/entry 6.4% = 16.3% of CPU0 spent on scheduling and timing machinery for a workload of three threads
magnitude_estimate: No direct fps. It resizes the target: it either raises the published 20.6 fps ceiling (making proposals 1 and 2 sufficient for the >=20 fps goal) or confirms it (making them insufficient). Given the review has 95 candidates all sized against that one constant, and that the constant rests on an instrument that cannot tell running from queued, this is the cheapest thing on the list that can change a verdict. One kernel build, one boot, no board risk.
rule_check: Kernel config only, on a diagnostic build. No app touched, nothing shipped, no feature disabled, no flash layout change. SCHEDSTATS adds no debugfs and no /proc/slabinfo-style dependency, so it does not reintroduce the 1.14 MB DEBUG_FS cost or the SLUB_TINY conflict.
prior_attempts: Recorded measurement traps note that /proc/stat over-counts 2.7x and that a 200 Hz SIGPROF wedges the board, and the project explicitly has no perf/ftrace/PMU — but SCHEDSTATS has never been tried, and 'the lens' notes never list runqueue wait among the things that were checked. waitsamp itself is only days old and its R-state conflation is not recorded anywhere.

title: The panel is 60 Hz, not 42, and the compositor's frame clock is 16 ms against its 16.67 ms — a 2.5 Hz beat
layer: lvdesk (with one value read from the DRM mode)
mechanism: lvdesk gates its LVGL pass and its poll deadline on a hard-coded '#define FRAME_MS 16 /* 60 Hz panel */'. The shipping panel runs at 25,623 kHz over htotal 861 x vtotal 496 = 59.9992 Hz, i.e. a 16.667 ms period. 16 against 16.667 is a 2.5 Hz beat: about every 400 ms the compositor produces two frames inside one panel period (one of which is never scanned out) or none, on a panel that free-runs with no vblank synchronisation and no double buffering. Read the period from the mode the driver already reports (the 'scanout started' line and the driver's frame_period) instead of hard-coding it, and round UP rather than down so the compositor never outruns the panel. Worth recording for the review as a whole: the '42 Hz panel' constant in the brief is stale — pclk_khz has defaulted to 25623 since the 60 Hz change, and the driver's own comments still quote 42.1 Hz in places, which is how the stale figure propagated.
evidence: lvdesk/lvdesk.c:8878 — '#define FRAME_MS 16 /* 60 Hz panel */', used at :10176 (frame_due) and :10228 (poll timeout)

linux-71-port/drivers/gpu/drm/espressif/esp32s31-lcd.c:631 — static unsigned int pclk_khz = 25623; and :1780-1783 — frame_period = htotal * vtotal * NSEC_PER_SEC / (clock * 1000); 25,623,000 / (861 * 496) = 59.9992 Hz = 16.667 ms

magnitude_estimate: Sub-1% on fullscreen throughput — fullscreen games bypass the LVGL pass entirely (fs_render_set pauses the refresh timer) so this does not touch the Quake or Doom timedemo. The effect is on the desktop and on the windowed canary's frame-gap tail, where one frame in every ~25 is produced into a period that cannot show it. Offered as a free correctness fix inside this sweep's remit, not as a win: it is one line plus a mode read, and it removes a periodic artefact from the instrument the rest of the review is measured with.
rule_check: lvdesk is ours. No app touched, no kernel change, no RAM, no flash, no feature disabled. Runtime-checkable: pclk_khz is writable at 0644, so the 42 Hz and 60 Hz cases can both be exercised on one boot.
prior_attempts: 'Lower panel refresh to free memory bandwidth' was measured (59/50/42/35 Hz, fps all inside the spread) — that tested the RATE, never the PHASE relationship between the compositor's clock and the panel's. prompt_flip (+19% on pointer motion) and the vblank-quantisation note both concern waiting FOR vblank, which is the opposite direction; this is about not running faster than it.

title: Overclock the CPU PLL: CPLL fb_div 8→10 takes the CPU and the whole memory domain from 320 to 400 MHz
layer: hart0 loader / ESP-IDF clock init (rtc_clk.c path), plus kernel DTS timebase-frequency and OpenSBI rebuild
mechanism: On the S31 the CPU clock is a plain integer multiple of the 40 MHz XTAL: clk_ll_cpll_set_freq_mhz() writes LP_CLKRST.cpll_div.cpll_fb_div = 8, ref_div = 1, giving CPLL = 320 MHz, and clk_ll_cpll_set_config() is a documented no-op ("CPLL frequency controlled by digital only on the target"). fb_div is an ordinary writable register field, so fb_div = 10 gives 400 MHz with no analog reconfiguration. Everything downstream is a divider off that root: MEM_CLK = HP_ROOT/{1,2} (1-bit field), SYS_CLK = CPU_CLK/N, APB_CLK = SYS_CLK/N. The vendor states the ceilings in rtc_clk_cpu_freq_to_cpll_mhz(): MEM_CLK ≤ 160 MHz, SYS_CLK ≤ 320/3 = 106.67 MHz, APB_CLK ≤ 320/6 = 53.33 MHz. At CPU 320 today, every one of those is already pinned at its maximum (mem_div 2 → 160, sys_div 3 → 106.67, apb_div 2 → 53.33) — there is no headroom anywhere except the PLL itself. At CPLL 400 with cpu_div 1, mem_div 2, sys_div 4, apb_div 2 you get CPU 400 (+25%), MEM 200, SYS 100 (legal, −6%), APB 50 (legal, −6%). The single out-of-spec item is MEM at 200 vs a stated 160 ceiling, because the MEM divider is one bit and cannot produce /3. Critically, this does NOT touch the external memory interfaces: clk_tree_defs.h says PSRAM's default source is MPLL and flash's is BBPLL(480), and SDMMC_CLK_SRC is MPLL — the 250 MHz octal PSRAM pin clock, the 80 MHz QIO flash clock and the SD clock are all independent of CPLL, so the calibrated MSPI timing point is not disturbed (and IDF re-runs mspi_timing_tuning at boot anyway). This is the only change found anywhere in the sweep that scales user code, kernel code, lvdesk and PSRAM latency together, which is exactly the shape the 16.4 → 20 fps gap needs.

/opt/esp-idf/components/soc/esp32s31/include/soc/clk_tree_defs.h:44-46, 373-414 — CPLL feeds CPU/MSPI-Flash/MSPI-PSRAM as a *selectable* source; PSRAM_CLK_SRC_DEFAULT = MPLL, flash uses BBPLL, SDMMC_CLK_SRC = MPLL
bootloader/sdkconfig — CONFIG_ESP_DEFAULT_CPU_FREQ_MHZ_320=y, CONFIG_SPIRAM_SPEED_250M=y, CONFIG_SPIRAM_MODE_OCT=y

magnitude_estimate: +25% on CPU clock and +25% on the MEM domain simultaneously. Quake's CPU0 is 59% user + 32% kernel + 9% idle with the main thread 86% busy; the part that is pure instruction issue scales 1:1 and the part that is PSRAM stall scales with MEM_CLK too, so a 15-25% fps gain is the honest band: 16.4 → 19-20.5 fps, i.e. the whole remaining gap to the 20 fps goal in one change. A gentler arm (fb_div 9 → 360 MHz, MEM 180) is +12.5% but forces SYS to 90 (−16%) or 120 (over ceiling), so 400 is actually the cleaner operating point.
rule_check: No application code touched — this is the loader's clock init plus a DTS constant. No feature disabled (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and audio all keep running; their PLLs are separate). No mature upstream code patched. Costs zero RAM. Apps stay on SD. Fully reversible: reflash hello_world.bin (the loader at 0x20000) plus the kernel; worst case the board fails to boot and is recovered by a reflash, which is the normal loop here. Two honest risks to state: (1) MEM_CLK at 200 MHz is 25% above the vendor's documented 160 MHz ceiling, so this is a genuine overclock of the cache/MSPI-controller domain and must be soak-tested for silent data corruption, not just for boot — use the existing canary plus a PSRAM integrity pass, because a marginal memory domain corrupts rather than hangs; (2) pmu_param.c carries a voltage table per operating point and 400 MHz may need the digital core voltage raised, which is where to look first if it boots but is unstable. Also note rtc_clk.c's warning that hardware may silently auto-correct an illegal *divider* — that applies to the divider path, not to fb_div, but read back and verify the achieved frequency (CoreMark and a known-rate timer) rather than trusting the register.
prior_attempts: Never attempted. The dead-end register contains no CPU-clock entry. Round 1 proposed raising the *flash* clock to 120 MHz (closed: 80 MHz is the S31 IDF maximum, header 'dio' string stale, flash already QIO-80 at 22-32 MB/s) and 'pin the MSPI PSRAM timing point' — both are about the external memory interfaces, which this proposal deliberately leaves alone. cpufreq was explored and found inert (hart0 holds 320 MHz always, 4,388 transitions changed nothing, performance governor shipped for jitter only) — but that work only ever moved the *divider* between the vendor's five preset operating points; nobody looked at the PLL that defines the top of that range. The 'AXI QoS' and 'AXI performance monitor' round-1 items are about arbitration on the fabric, not its frequency.

title: .text..fast is 276 KB against a 16 KB two-way instruction cache — the hot-text strategy is sized to the wrong resource, and the prelock may be pointed at the wrong I-cache entirely
layer: kernel linker script / section layout, plus drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c (I-cache selection)
mechanism: The shipped SMP kernel puts 0xc083aa90–0xc087f9e0 = 282,448 bytes into .text..fast. The S31's instruction cache is CACHE_L1_ICACHE_SIZE = 0x4000 (16 KiB), MAX_L1_ICACHE_WAY = 2, 64-byte lines — 128 sets, two ways. So the 'RAM text' region is 17x the cache that serves it, and with only two ways any two hot functions whose addresses differ by a multiple of 8 KiB evict each other on every call. That reframes the entire history of this lever as a capacity/conflict curve rather than a list of good and bad objects: softirq.o alone (~10 KB) gave −19.7% (675→542 µs); input+evdev (18 KB) gave +3.8%; the profiled #320 batch (43 KB) gave −5%; DRM commit (26.8 KB) <1%; handle+irqdesc *added* to softirq made it worse than softirq alone (605 vs 542 µs); reclaim at 97 KB, the net spine at 70 KB and timer+storage at 113 KB were all null or negative. Monotonically worse with size is exactly what a 16 KB two-way cache produces, and it means the −19.7% mechanism is real but is currently being diluted 27x. Second, separate finding: the port and IDF disagree about which I-cache serves what. drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c:76 defaults esp32s31_icache_map to ICACHE0 and comments that 'I-cache 0 is hart 0's, I-cache 1 is hart 1's', while the prelock/preload code hardcodes the ICACHE1 register offsets — but IDF's cache_ll_l1_get_bus() maps by *address target*, not by hart: a flash vaddr yields IBUS0|DBUS0 and a PSRAM vaddr yields IBUS1|DBUS0. If IDF is right, flash instruction fetch (the kernel's 4.38 MB of XIP text) goes through ICACHE0 and every prelock experiment done so far pinned lines in the cache that serves PSRAM instead — a silent no-op that would look exactly like 'prelock does nothing'. The hardware settles this in one run with no guessing: CACHE_L1_IBUS0_ACS_HIT_CNT / MISS_CNT and CACHE_L1_IBUS1_ACS_* are per-bus counters; run a flash-text-heavy loop on hart1 and read which pair moves. That same instrument then tells you, for the first time, the actual I-cache miss rate of .text..fast, which is the number the whole hot-text plan should have been sized against.

magnitude_estimate: The mechanism is already measured at −19.7% on syscall/IPC round trips for one 10 KB object. Kernel is 32% of CPU0 during Quake. If sizing the resident set to ~12-14 KB and laying it out to avoid 8 KiB-stride conflicts recovers that scale across the genuinely hot path instead of one object, 5-15% of kernel time is in reach = 2-5% of CPU0, i.e. ~0.3-0.8 fps. If the ICACHE0/ICACHE1 mismatch is real, it additionally unblocks prelock, which was previously judged from a null result that may never have been a real test. Small-to-medium on its own; its larger value is that it makes a whole family of already-attempted experiments interpretable instead of noise.
rule_check: Kernel-side only: a linker-script section list and a driver register offset. No app rebuild, no app config. No feature removed. Nothing upstream patched (vmlinux-xip.lds.S and drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c are both ours). RAM cost is bounded and in fact *reduced*: shrinking .text..fast from 276 KB to ~16 KB hands ~260 KB of PSRAM back, which matters on a 15.4 MB machine, and the same text still executes from flash. Note the port-tree rule: any change has to land in patches/ or it is not committed.
prior_attempts: Round 1 proposed 'function granular profile ordered hot text', 'use the I-cache prelock', 'pin the flash-resident spine' and 'use the L1 cache access counters' — all of which assume the current framing. What none of them say is the number: 276 KB of .text..fast against 16 KB of two-way cache. The dead-end register records every individual .text..fast arm but never plots them against size, and never records the cache geometry that explains the shape. The ICACHE0/ICACHE1 contradiction is not recorded anywhere. The memory note 'validate silent instruments' is exactly the failure mode this would be: a prelock that quietly pins the wrong cache and reports success.

title: Use the D-cache's hardware preload engine as a software prefetch primitive — the CPU gets no memory-level parallelism today
layer: kernel (a small preload helper in drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c, used by copy_to_user, the DRM damage copy and the swap-in path) plus lvdesk/xshim for userspace copies
mechanism: CPU PSRAM→PSRAM copy is measured at 102 MB/s. That is 627 ns per 64-byte line for one load and one store, against a measured PSRAM chase latency of 274-316 ns — i.e. exactly two fully serialised round trips per line, with zero overlap. This is an in-order core with no prefetch instruction, so the load miss stalls at use and nothing else is in flight. It is not the fabric: AXI_IC_MAX_OST_AR_S_n defaults to 15 outstanding reads per slave port (max 32), so the interconnect is not the throttle. What is available and unused is an explicit, asynchronous preload engine on the D-cache: CACHE_L1_DCACHE_PRELOAD_ADDR / _SIZE / _CTRL, wrapped by cache_ll_l1_dcache_preload(cache_id, vaddr, size, order) which is documented to 'start preload for the given region and not wait', with a separate cache_ll_l1_dcache_preload_wait_done(). The size field is 14 bits, so up to 16,383 bytes per request — enough to software-pipeline: issue a preload for block N+1, copy block N out of cache, repeat. Because the engine fills the cache rather than a separate buffer, there is no coherency work and no flush/invalidate pairing, which is what made GDMA mem2mem unattractive. If it removes the load-miss round trip and leaves the copy store-limited, 102 MB/s should move toward the ~204 MB/s the store side alone implies. The Linux port already drives the *I-cache* preload registers (esp32s31_icache_prelock() writes ICACHE1_PRELOAD_ADDR/SIZE/CTRL and spins on the self-clearing ENA bit), so the register idiom is proven in-tree; the D-cache equivalents have never been touched. Validate on rootfs/membw first with three arms (plain copy, preload-pipelined copy, and a preload-issued-but-unused control to price the register writes) before wiring it into any real path.

soc2/register/soc/icm_sys_axi_ic_reg.h:2727-2742 — AXI_IC_REG_MAX_OST_AR_S_0 default 15, 'limit the number of outstanding for slave port' (so the fabric allows deep parallelism the CPU never uses)

ESP32S31_PRELOAD_SIZE_MAX = GENMASK(13,0) — 16,383 bytes per request
magnitude_estimate: Up to ~2x on CPU PSRAM→PSRAM copies (102 → ~200 MB/s) if the model is right. End to end that is worth 2-5%: the copies it reaches are DIRTYFB (measured 2,196 µs/frame), copy_to_user on the read path, the swap-in page copy, and xshim's 77 KB request-boundary copy. It will NOT help the palette expand — at 768 KB written in 3,607 µs that path is already running at 213 MB/s, i.e. at the measured fill bandwidth, so it is destination-bandwidth-bound and has nothing to prefetch. Stating that explicitly is part of the value: it rules the largest per-frame cost out of this lever.
rule_check: Platform side only — a kernel helper and our own lvdesk/xshim. No app rebuild or config steering. No feature disabled. Nothing upstream patched. RAM cost zero. One real hazard to size in the microbenchmark before believing anything: the preload engine fills the shared 64 KB two-way D-cache, so an over-eager preload evicts the very data the CPU is about to use, and on a two-way cache that turns into thrash quickly — keep the pipeline block small (1-4 KB) and measure the control arm. Second hazard: the CACHE registers sit in the APB domain at 53.33 MHz, so three register writes per block are not free; if the block is too small the register cost exceeds the latency saved, which is the same shape as the 'offload isn't purchasable below 128 KB' result and must be priced, not assumed.
prior_attempts: Never attempted. The dead-end register has 'I-cache autoload via devmem from Linux' (the hart died instantly, twice) and 'autoload from the loader' (a no-op, the flag only applies when the cache is off) — that is the *automatic* prefetcher (CACHE_L1_DCACHE_AUTOLOAD_CTRL + SCT0-3), a different register block and a global boot-time toggle. Round 1's 'turn on the cache autoload prefetchers' and 'enable the I-cache hardware prefetcher' are the same autoload. Round 1's 'measure memory-level parallelism (the 102)' proposes to measure the number; this proposes the specific mechanism that changes it. Round 1's 'critical word first and early restart' is CACHE_L1_DCACHE_WRAP / MISS_DISABLE_ACCESS, which shortens a single miss rather than overlapping several. GDMA for the damage copy was tried and lost (10.6 vs 7.9 ms, gdma_copy off gave Doom +2%) — but a DMA engine pays a wake-up and a coherency round trip that a cache preload does not.

title: Every set_pte writes back one cache line over MMIO, under four spinlocks and two clock reads, to publish four bytes
layer: kernel: arch/riscv/include/asm/pgtable.h and drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c
mechanism: The port's set_pte() and set_pmd() call esp32s31_cache_writeback(__pa(ptep), sizeof(*ptep)) because the Sv32 hardware walker does not snoop the write-back D-cache. That lands in esp32s31_cache_range(), which per call does: ktime_get_ns(); raw_spin_lock_irqsave on a single global lock shared by both harts; four writel_relaxed (MAP, ADDR, SIZE, CTRL) plus wmb(); a spin on an MMIO read of SYNC_CTRL until SYNC_DONE; then the whole op again because 'ESP-IDF's S31 workaround repeats writeback-class sync requests'; mb(); unlock; then atomic64_inc + two atomic64_add. CONFIG_GENERIC_ATOMIC64=y on rv32, so each of those three is itself a hashed spinlock acquire/release with interrupts disabled — four lock pairs and two timer reads per PTE. The register block is in the APB domain at 53.33 MHz, so each polling read is a full 320→106.67→53.33 MHz round trip with the CPU stalled. Three things are wrong with this and each is separately fixable. (1) Granularity: a 64-byte line holds 16 PTEs, and set_ptes() loops __set_pte_at() per entry, so a 16-PTE fault-around batch issues sixteen identical writebacks of the same line. (2) Batching: kernel 7.1 has the lazy-MMU framework and the bulk callers — zap_pte_range, copy_pte_range, filemap_map_pages, move_ptes, change_pte_range — already bracket their loops with arch_enter/leave_lazy_mmu_mode(). Implementing those two hooks to accumulate a dirty range and issue one writeback at leave collapses a 512-entry teardown from 512 MMIO round trips to 64. Correctness is preserved because the walker only needs the line visible before the sfence.vma that makes the translation usable, which is after the batch. (3) Instrumentation: the ktime and atomic64 block has no #ifdef — it is in shipping DIAG=0 builds, on this path and on every DMA map/unmap for SD, Wi-Fi and the display, and the three shared atomic64 counters are a cross-hart contended line by construction. Put them behind a static_key or drop them.

title: Both caches are two-way — colour the pages, because conflict misses on this machine are a platform-side lever on app performance
layer: kernel page allocator / DRM and lvdesk buffer placement
mechanism: The ROM header fixes MAX_L1_ICACHE_WAY = 2 and MAX_L1_DCACHE_WAY = 2. That makes the 64 KiB D-cache 512 sets x 2 ways x 64 B and the 16 KiB I-cache 128 sets x 2 ways x 64 B — the lowest associativity in any realistic modern design, and it is an external-memory cache indexed by the flat 0x5xxxxxxx PSRAM address, which Linux maps identically to physical. So the cache set of every page is decided by the physical page number Linux hands out: 8 colours for the D-cache (paddr[14:12]) and 2 for the I-cache (paddr[12]). Linux's buddy allocator picks colours at random. With two ways, three concurrent streams that collide are not degraded, they are destroyed — each reference evicts the line the next one needs. On this board the colliding streams are concrete: lvdesk reads a 320x240 source and writes a 768 KB scanout destination while Quake's 10 MB heap and the kernel's own data share the same 512 sets, and hart0 runs Linux code on the same D-cache. This is a lever on app performance that never touches the app: the rules allow the platform to choose where a page lands physically, and on a two-way physically-indexed cache that choice is worth real cycles. The right first move is measurement, not implementation — extend rootfs/membw with a colour sweep (copy between buffers whose physical offset varies over the 8 D-cache colours, and a three-stream variant with a small LUT in the loop) and read CACHE_L1_DBUS0_ACS_HIT_CNT / MISS_CNT / CONFLICT_CNT across arms. The CONFLICT_CNT register existing at all says the hardware counts exactly this. If a colour-conflicted copy is materially slower than a colour-disjoint one, the lever is real and the cheap implementations follow: colour-align the scanout and damage buffers at allocation (a few lines in the DRM driver, zero RAM, no allocator surgery), and only then consider a colouring policy for user anonymous pages.

magnitude_estimate: Unknown until the membw colour sweep runs, and that is the point — the sweep itself is a 20-minute result that either opens or closes the family. Prior art on two-way physically-indexed caches puts page colouring at 0-15% depending on how conflict-bound the workload is; Quake's texture working set is mostly capacity-bound so the upper end is unlikely, but the frame path (source stream + destination stream + palette LUT + kernel data, four streams into two ways) is exactly the shape colouring fixes. Treat anything above ~5% as the optimistic tail and report the spread across 5+ runs per arm.
rule_check: Platform side only: buffer placement in our DRM driver and, optionally, an allocator policy. The app binary, its build and its config are untouched — Linux choosing a physical page is not app steering. No feature disabled, nothing upstream patched, and the cheap version (colour-aligning the scanout and damage buffers) costs at most one page of alignment slack on a memory-bound machine. The expensive version (a colouring policy in the buddy allocator) must be rejected if it fragments: on 15.4 MB with CMA already lent out, an allocator that refuses pages of the wrong colour will OOM before it wins, so any such arm needs MemAvailable and CmaFree watched alongside fps, per the watermark-boost OOM lesson. Measure with fresh boot per arm — the per-boot ±10% Quake lottery will swallow anything smaller than it otherwise.
prior_attempts: Never considered. Nothing in the dead-end register, docs/ or the memory notes mentions associativity, cache colouring or conflict misses; the standing model in CLAUDE.md and the memory notes is 'one shared D-cache, 64 KB, 64 B lines, fixed' with no way count, and 'Enlarge or reconfigure the caches from the loader' was closed on size alone ('L1 I is 16 KB, D is 64 KB, lines 64 B, all fixed; no L2'). Round 1's 'dump the D-cache tag array' and 'use the L1 cache access counters' propose reading the cache; neither proposes changing what lands in it. The write-combine note ('free for one stream, 18x for three') is the closest prior observation and is arguably this effect seen from the other side without a mechanism attached.

title: Every page of the XIP overlay costs a whole-I-cache flush at mmap time — flush_icache_pte's !pfn_valid branch is ungated
layer: kernel (arch/riscv/mm/cacheflush.c, asm/pgtable.h, fs/cramfs physmem path)
mechanism: The XIP overlay is mapped by remap_pfn_range() over the WHOLE vma at mmap time (fs/cramfs/inode.c:355-445, the comment at :406 'The entire vma is mappable' and the call at :411). remap_pte_range therefore issues one set_pte_at per 4 KB page, in a tight loop. riscv's __set_pte_at (arch/riscv/include/asm/pgtable.h:654-660) calls flush_icache_pte() for every PTE whose _PAGE_EXEC is set, and set_ptes() loops it per entry. Upstream flush_icache_pte is gated by the per-folio PG_dcache_clean bit, so a folio is flushed once ever. THIS PORT ADDED AN EARLY BRANCH IN FRONT OF THE GATE: cacheflush.c:100-112, '/* XIP cramfs text is mapped with remap_pfn_range() ... page_folio() would walk a wild pointer during execve */ if (!pfn_valid(pte_pfn(pte))) { flush_icache_mm(mm, false); return; }'. Flash PFNs are never valid under SPARSEMEM_STATIC (RAM base 0x50000000, XIP flash 0x40400000), so EVERY executable PTE of EVERY XIP-mapped binary and library takes the ungated path. flush_icache_mm (cacheflush.c:57-95) unconditionally does local_flush_icache_all() — a fence.i that throws away the whole 16 KB I-cache (bootloader/sdkconfig:2819 CONFIG_CACHE_L1_ICACHE_SIZE=0x4000) — and, when another hart is currently running the same mm (true for any SDL app: the audio thread), sbi_remote_fence_i() at :89, an M-mode ecall plus a cross-hart IPI on the ~165 us path. So mapping a 1,832 kB XIP binary = 458 whole-I-cache flushes inside one mmap() call, each one forcing the flash-resident fault/mapping code (mm/memory.o, cacheflush.o, drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.o are all XIP .text) to refetch itself at ~1.6 us per 64 B line from 80 MHz QIO. Every iteration of the loop runs with a cold I-cache that the previous iteration emptied. Fix, in order of size: (a) one line — return without flushing for the !pfn_valid case, because cramfs XIP flash is read-only, is never written by the CPU, and its physical contents cannot change under the mapping, so there is nothing to publish and no staleness to invalidate; (b) if paranoia demands a flush, do it once per vma in the mmap path instead of once per PTE. First experiment needs no kernel build and no board change beyond a tiny tool: time mmap() of the same XIP file with PROT_READ vs PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC — both take the remap_pfn_range path, only the exec one pays the flush storm.

title: The scheduler is told the two harts share no cache: SCHED_MC is compiled out, so sd_llc is NULL and every upstream co-location heuristic is dead code
layer: kernel config + DT (Makefile SLIM_TWEAKS, esp32s31.dtsi cpu nodes)
mechanism: The SMP build applies the size diet: Makefile:387 '--disable SCHED_MC', pulled into SMP_TWEAKS at :404, justified at :392-402 as 'scheduler topology levels that mean nothing on two identical harts'. Confirmed in the shipping config (line 444 CONFIG_ARCH_SUPPORTS_SCHED_MC=y, line 445 '# CONFIG_SCHED_MC is not set'). SD_SHARE_LLC is produced ONLY by cpu_core_flags(), which exists only under CONFIG_SCHED_MC (kernel/sched/topology.c:1784-1791); the remaining PKG level is registered with a NULL flags function (:1815). So no sched_domain carries SD_SHARE_LLC, sd_llc is NULL, sd_llc_id defaults to the CPU itself, and cpus_share_cache(0,1) (kernel/sched/core.c:3886-3892) returns FALSE — on a machine whose two harts share their ONLY D-cache (drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c:407-410: 'ONE shared D-cache, TWO I-caches'). Consequences, all in 7.1 source: (1) select_idle_sibling() does 'sd = per_cpu(sd_llc, target); if (!sd) return target;' (fair.c:8153-8155) — the idle scan never runs; (2) the 'previous CPU is cache affine and idle' shortcut at fair.c:8118 is gated on cpus_share_cache and never fires; (3) wake_affine_idle()'s first clause (fair.c:7607) never fires, so the only way a wakeup lands on the waker's CPU is the sync flag; (4) ttwu_queue_cond() (core.c:3929-3934) returns true immediately, so EVERY cross-CPU wakeup goes through the remote wakelist and an IPI — on the lent hart that is the ~165 us emulated-interrupt path, taken even when CPU1 is already running. Net effect: wakeups are sticky to prev_cpu, and the kernel's entire adaptive placement machinery is disabled on the one machine where the cache argument for it is strongest. Fix: --enable SCHED_MC (a few kB of a 140 kB margin), and correct the DT, which currently gives each hart its own 64 KB d-cache (esp32s31.dtsi:235 and :265) — describe the D-cache as shared (a common cache node referenced by next-level-cache) so cpu_coregroup_mask()/last_level_cache_is_shared() group the harts rather than splitting them. The same dtsi also claims i-cache-size 32768 where bootloader/sdkconfig:2819 says 0x4000, so the cache description is already known-wrong in one field.

title: The kernel's RAM image and all 281 kB of .text..fast run on 4 KB TLB entries while its flash text gets 4 MB leaves — setup_vm_final's ordering silently drops the port's own megapage mapping
layer: kernel (arch/riscv/mm/init.c, XIP linear/kernel mapping)
mechanism: create_kernel_page_table() (init.c:1001-1035) does exactly the right thing for XIP: flash text in PMD_SIZE (4 MB) leaves at :1022-1027, and the kernel's RAM image — which by the linker script is where .text..fast lives (vmlinux-xip.lds.S:441-470, the section sits between _sdata and __bss_start) — also in PMD_SIZE leaves at :1032-1035. But setup_vm_final calls create_linear_mapping_page_table() FIRST (init.c:1443) and create_kernel_page_table() second (:1447), and on rv32 the kernel is linked inside the linear map (KERNEL_LINK_ADDR == PAGE_OFFSET; va_pa_offset is defined at :1222-1226 to make the two agree — the code even says so at :1213-1220). create_linear_mapping_range uses best_map_size(), which returns PAGE_SIZE unconditionally unless CONFIG_64BIT (:751-769), so it fills every RAM pgd slot with a pointer to a 4 KB PTE table; create_pgd_mapping then installs a leaf ONLY IF THE SLOT IS EMPTY (:732-736), so the second call is a no-op for RAM. Result, verifiable in one boot from the page tables: 4.38 MB of flash text costs 2 ITLB entries, while the 281,568 bytes of .text..fast (worklog 2026-09-21) cost up to 69, and every kernel stack (no VMAP_STACK on rv32, so stacks come from the page allocator), every slab object, every page-cache page and every page-table page is a separate 4 KB entry. On this SoC a TLB miss is not cheap: asm/pgtable.h:639-650 states 'S31's Sv32 walker does not snoop the shared write-back D-cache' (which is why set_pte writes a cache line back on every PTE store), so a miss is two page-table reads that bypass the D-cache entirely, against a measured dependent-load latency through PSRAM of 275-316 ns. THIS IS THE ONE UNTESTED EXPLANATION FOR THE .text..fast SIZE CEILING: softirq.o alone is -19.7%, input+evdev (18 kB) +3.8%, but 33 kB of reclaim = null, 43 kB = -5%, 70-113 kB = null or worse — small batches win, big ones do not, which is what a small ITLB predicts and which the shipped 'D-cache pollution' story (lds.S:283-293, flagged there as unverified) does not explain, since instruction fetch from PSRAM is served by the private I-cache. Fix, narrow and cheap: memblock_mark_nomap() the 4 MB-aligned block holding the kernel image before the linear map (the exact idiom upstream already uses for STRICT_KERNEL_RWX at init.c:1374-1385), then map that block with a PGDIR_SIZE leaf; VA 0xC0800000 and PA 0x50000000 are both 4 MB aligned, so it is legal as-is. It also RETURNS RAM (one 4 KB PTE page per 4 MB mapped).

title: Adopt lazy MMU mode: every bulk page-table loop in the kernel is already bracketed for batching, and this port pays an MMIO round trip per PTE instead
layer: kernel (arch/riscv, asm/pgtable.h + drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c)
mechanism: Because the Sv32 walker does not snoop the D-cache, this port publishes every page-table store by hand: set_pte (asm/pgtable.h:639-650) and set_pmd (:256-266) call esp32s31_cache_writeback(__pa(ptep), 4). That helper (drivers/cache/esp32s31_cache.c:87-107, 160-186) takes a raw spinlock with IRQs off, writes MAP/ADDR/SIZE/CTRL, POLLS the CTRL register until SYNC_DONE, and then — because writeback-class syncs are issued twice on this SoC as an IDF workaround — writes CTRL and polls AGAIN. That is ~8 MMIO writes and at least 2 MMIO read-polls, IRQs off, on a peripheral bus, to publish FOUR BYTES. Linux already has the upstream mechanism for exactly this and 7.1 ships the modern nested version of it: CONFIG_ARCH_HAS_LAZY_MMU_MODE with lazy_mmu_mode_enable/disable/pause/resume and per-task state (include/linux/pgtable.h:248-355, mm/Kconfig:1454). Every bulk page-table loop in the tree is ALREADY bracketed by it — mm/memory.c:1275 (zap), :1925, :2922 (remap_pte_range, i.e. the XIP overlay mmap path), :3333; mm/vmalloc.c:112, :396, :563; mm/vmscan.c:3498, :3591, :4241; mm/mremap.c:263; mm/mprotect.c:340; mm/madvise.c:455, :677 — but riscv does not select the Kconfig symbol, so all of it compiles to nothing (:355-358). Implementing arch_enter/leave/flush_lazy_mmu_mode for this port (accumulate a [min,max] physical range in the task's lazy state; issue ONE writeback, and at most one I-cache flush, at leave) converts N MMIO round trips into 1 for fork's copy_pte_range, exit/munmap's zap_pte_range, every vmalloc map/unmap, mprotect, mremap, madvise and the reclaim walks — and, combined with proposal 1, collapses an XIP library mmap from hundreds of flush+MMIO pairs to one. Correctness: the deferred item is only the publish to memory for the hardware walker, so arch_flush_lazy_mmu_mode() must also be called from riscv's flush_tlb_* helpers (and the set_pte path must keep publishing immediately when the mode is inactive or in_interrupt(), which the generic API already guarantees).

Per PTE the saving is one lock + ~8 MMIO writes + 2 polls (order 0.5-1 us at peripheral-bus latency); fork/exec/exit of a desktop process touches thousands of PTEs, so single-digit milliseconds per process lifecycle, plus whatever the boot's 301 forks multiply that by. Its larger value is as the general fix behind proposal 1 and as the only clean way to stop paying a hardware sync per four bytes. Worth pairing with a check of whether the double-issue workaround is really unconditional in /opt/esp-idf — if it is not, every writeback in the system (including the ~614 kB per fullscreen present) halves.

Kernel-side, arch-port code, using an upstream API exactly as upstream intends; no application rebuilt or steered; apps stay on SD; no feature disabled; no mature upstream driver patched (the change is riscv arch code plus this project's own cache driver); costs a few bytes of per-task state, no meaningful RAM. Must-verify before shipping: arch_flush_lazy_mmu_mode() hooked into riscv TLB-flush helpers so a deferred publish can never be overtaken by an sfence.vma.
